chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 1 — London. An ante-chamber in the King’s palace
paragraphs: Enter the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Bishop of Ely.

CANTERBURY. My lord, let me tell you about that same bill that's being pushed again. It came up in the eleventh year of the last king's reign, and it would have passed against us. But the rowdy, unsettled times pushed it aside before it could be debated further.
ELY. But how can we fight it now, my lord?

CANTERBURY. We have to think about that. If it passes against us, we lose the better half of what we own. They would strip us of all the land that devout men have left to the Church in their wills. The bill values it like this: enough to support, to the King's honor, fifteen earls and fifteen hundred knights and six thousand two hundred good esquires. It would also pay for a hundred well-stocked almshouses to care for lepers, the old, and the poor who are too weak to work. And on top of that, a thousand pounds a year would go into the King's treasury. That is what the bill says.
ELY. That would drain us deeply.
CANTERBURY. It would drain the cup and swallow the cup too.
ELY. But how do we prevent it?
CANTERBURY. The King is full of grace and good will.
ELY. And a true friend of the holy Church.

CANTERBURY. His early years gave no sign of it. The moment his father's breath left his body, his wildness seemed to die as well, as if it had been put to death inside him. At that very instant, Reflection came down like an angel and whipped the sinful Adam out of him. It left his body like a paradise, ready to hold heavenly spirits. No one was ever made a scholar so suddenly. Reform never came in such a flood, with such a rushing current scouring away faults. And a many-headed Hydra of willfulness never lost its hold so fast and so completely as it did in this king.
ELY. We are lucky in the change.

CANTERBURY. Just listen to him reason about religion, and you would admire him so much that you'd secretly wish he were a bishop. Hear him debate affairs of state, and you would say he had studied nothing else. Listen to him talk of war, and a terrible battle is played for you like music. Bring him any political problem, and he will undo its Gordian knot as easily as untying his garter. When he speaks, the air itself, which is free to roam as it pleases, goes still, and silent wonder waits in men's ears to steal his sweet, honeyed phrases. So practical experience of life must have been the teacher of this theory. It is astonishing how his Grace picked it up, since he was devoted to idle pursuits. His companions were uneducated, crude and shallow, and his hours were filled with brawls, banquets and sports. No one ever saw in him any study, or any retreat or separation from the public haunts and the common crowd.

ELY. The strawberry grows best under the nettle, and wholesome berries ripen best next to fruit of a lower kind. In the same way the Prince hid his thoughtful side behind a veil of wildness. No doubt it grew like summer grass, fastest at night, unseen but steadily growing in strength.
CANTERBURY. It must be so, because miracles have ended. So we have to admit there is some ordinary means by which things are brought to perfection.
ELY. But, my good lord, what about easing this bill that the Commons are pressing? Is his Majesty inclined to it or not?

CANTERBURY. He seems neutral. Or rather he leans more toward our side than toward those who brought the bill against us. I have made an offer to his Majesty, on behalf of our assembled clergy and because of matters now in hand, which I have explained to his Grace in full, concerning France. I offered a larger sum than the clergy has ever given to any of his predecessors at one time.
ELY. How did he receive this offer, my lord?

CANTERBURY. His Majesty accepted it well. But there was not enough time for him to hear what I could see he wanted to hear: the detailed and plain account of his true claims to certain dukedoms, and in general to the crown and throne of France, descended from Edward, his great-grandfather.
ELY. What interrupted this?
CANTERBURY. The French ambassador asked for an audience just then, and I think the hour has come to hear him. Is it four o'clock?
ELY. It is.
CANTERBURY. Then let's go in and learn his message. I could guess it right now, before the Frenchman says a word.
ELY. I'll follow you, and I'm eager to hear it.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 2 — The same. The presence chamber
paragraphs: Enter King Henry, Gloucester, Bedford, Clarence, Warwick, Westmorland, Exeter and Attendants.
KING HENRY. Where is my gracious Lord of Canterbury?
EXETER. He isn't here in the room.
KING HENRY. Send for him, good uncle.
WESTMORLAND. Shall we call in the ambassador, my liege?
KING HENRY. Not yet, my cousin. Before we hear him, we want some weighty matters settled. They are weighing on our mind, and they concern us and France.
Enter the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Bishop of Ely.
CANTERBURY. May God and his angels guard your sacred throne, and may you fill it for many years!

KING HENRY. We thank you, truly. My learned lord, we ask you to go on and explain, justly and with a clear religious conscience, whether the Salic law they have in France does or does not bar our claim. And God forbid, my dear and faithful lord, that you should twist, strain or bend your reading of it. God forbid that you should burden your conscience by laying out claims that are falsely made, whose right does not fit the truth in its natural colors. For God knows how many men now in good health will shed their blood to prove whatever your reverence urges us to. So take care how you pledge our person, and how you wake our sleeping sword of war. We charge you in God's name, take care. Two such kingdoms have never fought without much bloodshed. Every innocent drop of it is a grief and a bitter complaint against the man whose wrongs sharpen the swords that cause such waste of short human lives. Under this solemn charge, speak, my lord. We will listen, take note, and believe in our heart that what you say has been washed in your conscience as pure as a sin washed away by baptism.

CANTERBURY. Then hear me, gracious sovereign, and hear me, you peers, who owe yourselves, your lives and your service to this imperial throne. There is only one bar to your Highness's claim to France, and it is the one they take from Pharamond: _In terram Salicam mulieres ne succedant_, "No woman shall succeed in Salic land." The French wrongly twist "Salic land" to mean the realm of France, and Pharamond to be the founder of this law barring women. Yet their own writers honestly state that the Salic land is in Germany, between the rivers Sala and Elbe. There Charles the Great, after conquering the Saxons, left behind and settled some Frenchmen. They looked down on the German women for the shameless way some of them lived, and so they made this law: no woman should inherit in Salic land. This Salic land, as I said, lies between the Elbe and the Sala, and today it is called Meissen in Germany. So it is plain that the Salic law was not made for the realm of France. Nor did the French hold the Salic land until four hundred and twenty-one years after the death of King Pharamond, whom they foolishly suppose to be the founder of this law. He died in the year of our redemption four hundred and twenty-six. Charles the Great conquered the Saxons and settled the French beyond the river Sala in the year eight hundred and five. Besides, their own writers say that King Pepin, who deposed Childeric, claimed the crown of France as heir general, since he was descended from Blithild, daughter of King Clothair. Hugh Capet also seized the crown from Charles, Duke of Lorraine, the only male heir of the true line of Charles the Great. To give his title some look of truth, though in pure truth it was rotten and worthless, Capet presented himself as heir to the Lady Lingare, daughter of Charlemain, who was the son of Lewis the Emperor, who was the son of Charles the Great. Also King Lewis the Tenth, sole heir of the usurper Capet, could not rest easy in his conscience while wearing the crown of France. He needed to be satisfied that his grandmother, the fair Queen Isabel, was a direct descendant of the Lady Ermengare, daughter of that same Charles, Duke of Lorraine. By that marriage the line of Charles the Great was joined again to the crown of France. So, as clear as the summer sun, King Pepin's title, Hugh Capet's claim and King Lewis's satisfaction all rest on rights held through a woman. And so do the kings of France to this day. Even so, they would hold up this Salic law to bar your Highness from claiming through a woman. They would rather hide in a net of excuses than openly set aside their own crooked titles, which they took from you and your ancestors.
KING HENRY. Can I make this claim with right and a clear conscience?

CANTERBURY. Let the sin be on my head, dread sovereign! For in the Book of Numbers it is written, "When a man dies, let the inheritance pass to his daughter." Gracious lord, stand up for what is yours! Unfurl your bloody flag! Look back to your mighty ancestors! Go, my dread lord, to the tomb of your great-grandfather, from whom you claim, and call up his warlike spirit. Call up your great-uncle's too, Edward the Black Prince. On French soil he played out a tragedy, defeating the full power of France, while his mighty father stood smiling on a hill to watch his lion's cub feed on the blood of the French nobility. Oh, noble English, who could meet the full pride of France with half their forces and let the other half stand laughing by, idle and cold for lack of action!

ELY. Wake the memory of these brave dead, and renew their deeds with your mighty arm. You are their heir. You sit on their throne. The blood and courage that made them famous run in your veins. And my thrice-mighty liege is in the very May morning of his youth, ripe for great exploits and enterprises.
EXETER. Your fellow kings and monarchs of the earth all expect you to rouse yourself, as the lions of your blood did before you.

WESTMORLAND. They know your Grace has the cause, the means and the might, and so you do. No King of England ever had richer nobles or more loyal subjects. Their hearts have left their bodies here in England and are already camped in the fields of France.

CANTERBURY. Oh, let their bodies follow, my dear liege, with blood and sword and fire to win your right! To help this, we of the clergy will raise for your Highness a sum so large that the clergy has never at one time brought as much to any of your ancestors.
KING HENRY. We must not only arm to invade the French. We must also set aside forces to defend against the Scot, who will raid us at every advantage.
CANTERBURY. The people of those border regions, gracious sovereign, will be wall enough to defend our inland from the thieving borderers.

KING HENRY. We don't only mean the roving snatchers. We fear the Scot's main design, for he has always been a fickle neighbor to us. You will read that my great-grandfather never went into France with his forces without the Scot pouring down on his unguarded kingdom like the tide through a breach, with the whole brimming fullness of his strength. He galled the stripped land with fierce attacks and ringed castles and towns with a grim siege. England, empty of defense, shook and trembled at such a bad neighbor.

CANTERBURY. Then she has been more feared than harmed, my liege. Look at her own example. When all her knights were in France and she was a mourning widow of her nobles, she not only defended herself well. She also captured the King of Scots and locked him up like a stray animal. She sent him to France to fill King Edward's fame with captive kings, and to make her chronicle as rich with praise as the ooze at the sea's bottom is rich with sunken wrecks and countless treasures.

WESTMORLAND. But there's a very old and true saying: "If you want to win France, begin with Scotland first." For once the eagle England is out hunting, the weasel Scot sneaks into her unguarded nest and sucks her royal eggs. He plays the mouse while the cat is away, and tears and wrecks more than he can eat.

EXETER. It follows, then, that the cat must stay home. Yet that is a forced necessity, since we have locks to protect our valuables and neat traps to catch petty thieves. While the armed hand fights abroad, the careful head defends itself at home. For government, though it is divided into high, low and lower parts, keeps in one agreement and joins in a full and natural close, like music.

CANTERBURY. That is why heaven divides the state of man into different functions. It keeps effort in constant motion, and fixes obedience as its aim and target. Honey-bees work this way. They are creatures that teach, by a rule of nature, the art of order to a populous kingdom. They have a king and officers of various kinds. Some, like magistrates, keep order at home. Others, like merchants, venture out to trade abroad. Others, like soldiers armed with their stings, plunder the summer's velvet buds and bring the loot home in a merry march to the royal tent of their emperor. He is busy in his majesty and watches the singing masons building roofs of gold, the civil citizens kneading the honey, and the poor laboring porters crowding their heavy loads in at his narrow gate. He sees the sad-eyed judge, with his surly hum, handing the lazy, yawning drone over to pale executioners. From this I conclude that many things, all pointing to one agreement, can work in opposite ways. Many arrows, shot in different directions, reach one mark. Many roads meet in one town. Many fresh streams meet in one salt sea. Many lines meet at the center of a sundial. So many thousands of actions, once started, can end in one purpose and all be carried through without failure. Therefore, to France, my liege! Divide your happy England into four, take one quarter with you into France, and you alone will make all Gaul shake. If we, with three times that strength left at home, cannot defend our own doors from the dog, then let us be torn apart and let our nation lose its name for toughness and good sense.
KING HENRY. Call in the messengers sent from the Dauphin.
[_Exeunt some Attendants._]

Now we are firmly decided. By God's help, and yours, the noble sinews of our power, once France is ours we will bend it to our will or break it to pieces. Either we will sit there ruling over France and all her almost kingly dukedoms with wide and ample power, or we will lay these bones in an unworthy urn, tombless, with no memorial over them. Either our history will speak of our deeds freely and with a full mouth, or our grave will have a tongueless mouth, like a Turkish mute, with not even a wax-written epitaph to honor it.
Enter Ambassadors of France.
Now we are well prepared to learn the pleasure of our fair cousin the Dauphin. For we hear your greeting is from him, not from the King.
FIRST AMBASSADOR. May it please your Majesty to give us leave to deliver freely what we have been charged with? Or shall we only hint at the Dauphin's meaning and our message from far off?

KING HENRY. We are no tyrant but a Christian king. Our anger is as much under the control of our mercy as the wretches chained in our prisons. So tell us the Dauphin's mind with frank and unrestrained plainness.

AMBASSADOR. Then, in short: your Highness recently sent word into France claiming certain dukedoms, by the right of your great predecessor, King Edward the Third. In answer to this claim, the prince our master says you smack too much of your youth. He tells you to understand that nothing in France can be won with a nimble dance step. You cannot party your way into dukedoms there. So he sends you this barrel of treasure, which is better suited to your spirit. In return, he asks that the dukedoms you claim hear no more from you. This is what the Dauphin says.
KING HENRY. What treasure, uncle?
EXETER. Tennis-balls, my liege.

KING HENRY. We are glad the Dauphin is so playful with us. We thank you for his gift and for your trouble. When we have matched our rackets to these balls, we will play a set in France, by God's grace, that will knock his father's crown into the hazard. Tell him he has made a match with such a quarrelsome player that all the courts of France will be disturbed with chases. And we understand him well, the way he throws our wilder days in our face without weighing what use we made of them. We never valued this poor seat of England. So, living away from it, we gave ourselves over to wild license, as it is common that men are merriest when they are away from home. But tell the Dauphin I will keep my royal state, act like a king, and spread the sail of my greatness when I rouse myself on my throne of France. Because I have put aside my majesty and plodded like a working man on working days. But I will rise there in such full glory that I will dazzle every eye in France, and strike the Dauphin blind to look at us. And tell the playful prince that this mock of his has turned his balls into cannonballs. His soul will be heavily charged for the wasteful vengeance that will fly with them. For this mock of his will mock many thousands of widows out of their dear husbands, mock mothers out of their sons, and mock castles down. And some who are not yet conceived or born will have cause to curse the Dauphin's scorn. But all this lies in the will of God, to whom I appeal, and in whose name you can tell the Dauphin I am coming on, to avenge myself as I can and to put forth my rightful hand in a well-blessed cause. So go in peace, and tell the Dauphin his jest will taste only of shallow wit, when thousands weep more than ever laughed at it. — Escort them with safe conduct. — Farewell.
[_Exeunt Ambassadors._]
EXETER. This was a merry message.

KING HENRY. We hope to make the sender blush at it. So, my lords, let no good hour pass that can help our expedition. We have no thought in us now but France, except for those we owe to God, which come before our business. So let our forces for this war be gathered soon, and let everything be thought of that can add more feathers to our wings with reasonable speed. For, God before us, we'll scold this Dauphin at his father's door. So let every man now put his mind to work, so that this fair undertaking can be set in motion.
[_Exeunt._]
Flourish. Enter Chorus.

CHORUS. Now all the youth of England are on fire, and silken idleness lies in the wardrobe. Now the armorers thrive, and thoughts of honor rule alone in every man's heart. They sell the pasture now to buy the horse. They follow the model of all Christian kings, with winged heels, like English Mercuries. For now Expectation sits in the air and covers a sword from hilt to point with imperial crowns, crowns and coronets, promised to Harry and his followers. The French, warned by good intelligence of this most dreadful preparation, shake in fear and, with pale cunning, try to turn aside the English plans. Oh England! Model of inward greatness, like a little body with a mighty heart, what could you do, as honor would have you do, if all your children were loyal and true to their nature! But see your fault! France has found in you a nest of hollow hearts, and fills them with treacherous gold. Three corrupted men have, for French gold, confirmed a conspiracy with fearful France. They are Richard, Earl of Cambridge, Henry, Lord Scroop of Masham, and Sir Thomas Grey, knight of Northumberland. Oh guilt indeed! By their hands this grace of kings must die, if hell and treason keep their promises, before he takes ship for France, at Southampton. Hold your patience a little longer, and we'll make the best of the stretching of distance and force a play out of it. The money is paid, the traitors are agreed, the King has set out from London, and the scene is now carried, gentles, to Southampton. That is the playhouse now, and there you must sit. From there we shall carry you safely to France, and bring you back, charming the narrow seas to give you a gentle crossing. For if we can, we will not offend one stomach with our play. But until the King comes forth, and not before, we shift our scene to Southampton.
[_Exit._]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 1 — London. A street
paragraphs: Enter Corporal Nym and Lieutenant Bardolph.
BARDOLPH. Well met, Corporal Nym.
NYM. Good morning, Lieutenant Bardolph.
BARDOLPH. So, are you and Ancient Pistol friends yet?

NYM. For my part, I don't care. I say little. But when the time is right, there will be smiles, though that will be as it may. I don't dare fight, but I'll squint and hold out my iron. It's a plain one, but so what? It will toast cheese, and it will stand the cold as well as any other man's sword. And that's the end of it.
BARDOLPH. I'll pay for a breakfast to make you friends, and all three of us will be sworn brothers on the way to France. Let's do that, good Corporal Nym.
NYM. Honestly, I'll live as long as I can, that's for certain. And when I can't live any longer, I'll do what I can. That's my last stake, that's where it all ends up.
BARDOLPH. It's certain, Corporal, that he is married to Nell Quickly. And she certainly wronged you, because you were promised to her.

NYM. I can't say. Things must be as they may. Men may sleep, and still have their throats on them at the time. And some say knives have edges. It must be as it may. Patience may be a tired mare, but she'll keep plodding. There must be an outcome. Well, I can't say.
Enter Pistol and Hostess.
BARDOLPH. Here comes Ancient Pistol and his wife. Good Corporal, be patient here. Hello there, mine host Pistol!
PISTOL. Base cur, do you call me host? Now, by this hand, I swear I scorn the word. Nor shall my Nell keep lodgers.

HOSTESS. No, by my word, not for long. We can't lodge and feed a dozen or fourteen gentlewomen who make an honest living with the prick of their needles without people at once thinking we run a brothel. [_Nym and Pistol draw._] Oh, alas, Our Lady, if he isn't drawing his sword now! We'll see deliberate adultery and murder committed.
BARDOLPH. Good Lieutenant! Good Corporal! Start nothing here.
NYM. Pish!
PISTOL. Pish for you, Iceland dog! You prick-eared cur of Iceland!
HOSTESS. Good Corporal Nym, show your courage, and put away your sword.
NYM. Will you shove off? I want you _solus_, alone.

PISTOL. _Solus_, you outrageous dog! Oh, vile viper! I throw the _solus_ in your marvelous face. I throw the _solus_ in your teeth and in your throat, in your hateful lungs, yes, in your belly, by God, and, what's worse, in your nasty mouth! I hurl the _solus_ back into your guts. For I can take it, and Pistol's hammer is cocked, and flashing fire will follow.

NYM. I'm not Barbason, you can't conjure me. I have a mind to knock you about, fairly well. If you get nasty with me, Pistol, I'll scour you with my rapier, as best I can, in fair terms. If you'd step away, I'd prick your guts a little, in good terms, as best I can. And that's my mood.
PISTOL. Oh, vile braggart and damned furious wretch! The grave gapes open, and doting death is near. So breathe your last.
BARDOLPH. Hear me, hear what I say. Whoever strikes the first blow, I'll run him through up to the hilt, as I'm a soldier.
[_Draws._]
PISTOL. An oath of mighty force, and my fury will cool. Give me your fist, give me your forefoot. Your spirits are lofty indeed.
NYM. I will cut your throat, one time or another, in fair terms. That's my mood.

PISTOL. "Couple a gorge!" That is the word: cut the throat. I defy you again. Oh, hound of Crete, do you think you'll get my wife? No! Go to the hospital, and from the sweating tub of infamy fetch out the leprous kite of Cressida's kind, Doll Tearsheet by name, and take her as your wife. I have, and I will keep, the former Mistress Quickly as my only woman. And _pauca_, few words, that's enough. Go on.
Enter the Boy.

BOY. Mine host Pistol, you must come to my master, and you too, hostess. He is very sick and wants to go to bed. Good Bardolph, put your face between his sheets and do the job of a warming-pan. Honestly, he's very ill.
BARDOLPH. Away, you rogue!
HOSTESS. By my word, he'll be giving the crow a pudding one of these days. The King has killed his heart. Good husband, come home right now.
[_Exeunt Hostess and Boy._]
BARDOLPH. Come, shall I make you two friends? We have to go to France together. Why the devil should we keep knives to cut each other's throats?
PISTOL. Let floods overswell, and let fiends howl for food!
NYM. Will you pay me the eight shillings I won from you at betting?
PISTOL. Base is the slave who pays.
NYM. That I will have now. That's my mood.
PISTOL. As manhood shall settle it. Thrust home.
[_They draw._]
BARDOLPH. By this sword, whoever makes the first thrust, I'll kill him. By this sword, I will.
PISTOL. Sword is an oath, and oaths must run their course.
BARDOLPH. Corporal Nym, if you want to be friends, be friends. If you don't, then be enemies with me too. Please, put it away.
NYM. Shall I have my eight shillings I won from you at betting?

PISTOL. A noble you shall have, paid on the spot. And I'll give you drink as well, and friendship and brotherhood will join us. I'll live by Nym, and Nym shall live by me. Isn't that fair? For I shall be the camp's sutler, and profits will follow. Give me your hand.
NYM. Shall I have my noble?
PISTOL. Paid fairly in cash.
NYM. Well, then, that's my mood.
Enter Hostess.
HOSTESS. As you ever came from a woman, come in quickly to Sir John. Ah, poor heart! He is so shaken with a burning daily-and-every-third-day fever that it's pitiful to see. Dear men, come to him.
NYM. The King has run bad humors onto the knight. That's the plain of it.
PISTOL. Nym, you've spoken right. His heart is broken and strengthened.
NYM. The King is a good king. But it must be as it may. He puts up with some moods and gallops.
PISTOL. Let us comfort the knight. For, lambkins, we will live.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 2 — Southampton. A council-chamber
paragraphs: Enter Exeter, Bedford and Westmorland.
BEDFORD. By God, his Grace is bold to trust these traitors.
EXETER. They will be arrested very soon.
WESTMORLAND. How smooth and calm they carry themselves! As if loyalty sat in their hearts, crowned with faith and steady allegiance.
BEDFORD. The King knows all they plan. He found out by an interception they never dreamed of.
EXETER. Yes, but think of the man who shared his bed, whom he has dulled and sickened with gracious favors. That he should sell his sovereign's life to death and treachery for foreign money!
Trumpets sound. Enter King Henry, Scroop, Cambridge and Grey.

KING HENRY. Now the wind is fair, and we will go aboard. My Lord of Cambridge, my kind Lord of Masham, and you, my gentle knight, give me your thoughts. Don't you think the forces we bring with us will cut their way through the power of France, and carry out the task for which we have gathered them?
SCROOP. No doubt, my liege, if each man does his best.

KING HENRY. I don't doubt that, since we are sure that we take with us no heart that doesn't grow in fair agreement with ours. And we leave behind none that doesn't wish success and conquest to attend us.
CAMBRIDGE. No monarch was ever better feared and loved than your Majesty. I think there isn't a subject who sits in heartache and unease under the sweet shade of your rule.
GREY. True. Those who were your father's enemies have soaked their bitterness in honey, and serve you with hearts made of duty and zeal.
KING HENRY. Then we have great cause to be thankful. And we will forget how to use our hand sooner than we will forget to repay deserving service, according to its weight and worth.
SCROOP. Then service will toil with steeled sinews, and labor will refresh itself with hope, to give your Grace unending service.

KING HENRY. We expect no less. Uncle Exeter, set free the man who was jailed yesterday for railing against our person. We consider that it was too much wine that set him on, and on second thought we pardon him.
SCROOP. That is mercy, but too much carelessness. Let him be punished, sovereign, in case your letting him off breeds more of his kind.
KING HENRY. Oh, let us still be merciful.
CAMBRIDGE. Your Highness may be, and still punish too.
GREY. Sir, you show great mercy if you give him his life after a good taste of punishment.

KING HENRY. Alas, your too great love and care for me weigh heavily as prayers against this poor wretch! If little faults that come from drink are not to be winked at, how shall we open our eyes when capital crimes, chewed, swallowed and digested, appear before us? We will set that man free anyway, though Cambridge, Scroop and Grey, in their dear care and tender protection of our person, would have him punished. And now to our French business. Who are the recent commissioners?
CAMBRIDGE. I am one, my lord. Your Highness told me to ask for it today.
SCROOP. So you told me, my liege.
GREY. And me, my royal sovereign.

KING HENRY. Then, Richard, Earl of Cambridge, there is yours. There is yours, Lord Scroop of Masham. And, sir knight, Grey of Northumberland, this one is yours. Read them, and know that I know your worth. My Lord of Westmorland, and uncle Exeter, we will go aboard tonight. — Why, what is this, gentlemen! What do you see in those papers that makes you lose so much color? — Look how they change! Their cheeks are paper. — Why, what do you read there, that has so cowed your blood and chased it out of sight?
CAMBRIDGE. I confess my fault, and I submit myself to your Highness's mercy.
GREY, SCROOP. To which we all appeal.

KING HENRY. The mercy that was alive in us only a moment ago has been suppressed and killed by your own advice. For shame, you must not dare to talk of mercy, because your own arguments turn back on you, as dogs turn on their masters, and tear at you. See, my princes and my noble peers, these English monsters! My Lord of Cambridge here, you know how readily our love agreed to supply him with everything that belonged to his honor. And this man, for a few light crowns, lightly conspired and swore himself to the schemes of France to kill us here at Southampton. This knight, bound to us by our generosity no less than Cambridge is, has sworn the same. But oh, what shall I say to you, Lord Scroop? You cruel, ungrateful, savage and inhuman creature! You who carried the key to all my counsels, who knew the very bottom of my soul, who could almost have coined me into gold if you had wanted to use me for your own profit. Is it possible that foreign pay could draw out of you one spark of evil that might hurt my finger? It is so strange that, though the truth of it stands out as plain as black and white, my eye can scarcely see it. Treason and murder always kept together, like two devils yoked and sworn to each other's purpose. They worked so openly, for such natural causes, that no one cried out in wonder at them. But you, against all proportion, brought wonder in to wait on treason and murder. And whatever cunning fiend it was that worked on you so perversely has won the prize in hell for excellence. Other devils who tempt men to treason botch and bungle up damnation with patches, colors and forms borrowed from glittering shows of piety. But he who shaped you told you to stand up. He gave you no reason to commit treason, except to dub you with the name of traitor. If that same demon who has fooled you so were to walk the whole world with his lion's stride, he could go back to vast Tartarus and tell the legions, "I can never win a soul so easily as that Englishman's." Oh, how you have infected the sweetness of trust with suspicion! Do men seem dutiful? Why, so did you. Do they seem serious and learned? Why, so did you. Do they come from noble families? Why, so did you. Do they seem religious? Why, so did you. Or are they sparing in diet, free from crude passion, whether of mirth or anger, steady in spirit, not swerving with their blood, dressed and adorned in modest manners, not trusting the eye without the ear, and trusting neither except after purified judgment? You seemed such, and so finely sifted. And so your fall has left a kind of blot that casts some suspicion on the fullest and best-endowed man. I will weep for you. For this revolt of yours, I think, is like a second fall of man. Their faults are plain. Arrest them to answer to the law. And may God acquit them of their plots!

EXETER. I arrest you for high treason, by the name of Richard, Earl of Cambridge. I arrest you for high treason, by the name of Henry, Lord Scroop of Masham. I arrest you for high treason, by the name of Thomas Grey, knight, of Northumberland.
SCROOP. God has justly exposed our plans, and I repent my fault more than I fear my death. I beg your Highness to forgive it, though my body pays the price.

CAMBRIDGE. As for me, the gold of France did not seduce me, though I did accept it as a motive to carry out what I intended sooner. But thanks be to God for preventing it. I will gladly rejoice in that while I suffer, begging God and you to pardon me.

GREY. No faithful subject ever rejoiced more at the discovery of the most dangerous treason than I rejoice over myself at this hour, kept back from a damned enterprise. Pardon my fault, sovereign, but not my body.

KING HENRY. May God acquit you in his mercy! Hear your sentence. You conspired against our royal person. You joined with an openly declared enemy and received from his coffers the golden down payment for our death. In this you would have sold your king to slaughter, his princes and peers to slavery, his subjects to oppression and contempt, and his whole kingdom to ruin. As for our own person, we seek no revenge. But we must so cherish the safety of our kingdom, whose ruin you sought, that we hand you over to her laws. So go from here, poor miserable wretches, to your death. May God in his mercy give you patience to endure the taste of it, and true repentance for all your grievous offenses! Take them away.
[_Exeunt Cambridge, Scroop and Grey, guarded._]

Now, lords, to France. The enterprise will be as glorious for you as for us. We have no doubt of a fair and lucky war, since God has so graciously brought to light this dangerous treason lurking in our path to hinder our beginnings. We now have no doubt that every obstacle is smoothed from our way. Then forward, dear countrymen! Let us put our power into the hand of God and set it to work at once. Cheerfully to sea! Raise the signs of war! No king of England, if not king of France!
[_Flourish. Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 3 — London. Before a tavern
paragraphs: Enter Pistol, Nym, Bardolph, Boy and Hostess.
HOSTESS. Please, honey, sweet husband, let me walk you as far as Staines.
PISTOL. No. My manly heart is grieving. Bardolph, cheer up. Nym, rouse your boasting blood. Boy, bristle up your courage. Falstaff is dead, and we must grieve for him.
BARDOLPH. I wish I were with him, wherever he is, in heaven or in hell!

HOSTESS. No, surely he's not in hell. He's in Arthur's bosom, if any man ever went to Arthur's bosom. He made a finer end, and went off like any newly christened child. He died just between twelve and one, right at the turning of the tide. After I saw him fumbling with the sheets, and playing with flowers, and smiling at his fingertips, I knew there was only one way it could go. His nose was as sharp as a pen, and he babbled of green fields. "How now, Sir John!" I said. "Come, man, be of good cheer!" Then he cried out, "God, God, God!" three or four times. To comfort him, I told him he shouldn't think of God. I hoped there was no need to trouble himself with such thoughts yet. So he told me to put more covers on his feet. I put my hand into the bed and felt them, and they were as cold as any stone. Then I felt up to his knees, and higher and higher, and everything was as cold as stone.
NYM. They say he cried out against sack.
HOSTESS. Yes, he did.
BARDOLPH. And against women.
HOSTESS. No, he did not.
BOY. Yes, he did. He said they were devils incarnate.
HOSTESS. He could never stand carnation. It was a color he never liked.
BOY. He said once that the devil would have him because of women.
HOSTESS. He did handle women, in a way, to be sure. But by then he was rheumatic, and he talked about the whore of Babylon.
BOY. Don't you remember how he saw a flea sitting on Bardolph's nose, and said it was a black soul burning in hellfire?
BARDOLPH. Well, the fuel that kept that fire going is gone. That's all the riches I got out of serving him.
NYM. Shall we move? The King is about to leave Southampton.

PISTOL. Come, let's go. My love, give me your lips. Look after my belongings and my goods. Let common sense rule. The word is "Pay as you go." Trust no one. Oaths are straw, and men's promises are wafer-cakes. Holding fast is the only dog, my duck. So let _Caveto_, "beware," be your counselor. Go, wipe your eyes. Comrades in arms, let's go to France. Like horse-leeches, my boys, we'll suck, suck, suck the very blood!
BOY. And that's unhealthy food, they say.
PISTOL. Kiss her soft mouth, and march.
BARDOLPH. Goodbye, Hostess.
[_Kissing her._]
NYM. I can't kiss. That's my mood. But goodbye.
PISTOL. Let her show she's a good housewife. Keep close, I command you.
HOSTESS. Goodbye, farewell.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 4 — France. The King’s palace
paragraphs: Flourish. Enter the French King, the Dauphin, the Dukes of Berry and Brittany, the Constable and others.

FRENCH KING. So the English come against us with their full strength. It matters more than ever that we answer them like a king, with strong defenses. So the Dukes of Berry and Brittany, of Brabant and Orleans, must go out, and you, Prince Dauphin, with all quick speed, to line and repair our fortified towns with brave men and the means to defend them. England is advancing on us as fiercely as water rushing into a whirlpool. We must be as careful as our fears can teach us from the recent examples left on our fields by the English, whom we neglected and who proved fatal.

DAUPHIN. My most feared father, it is right that we arm ourselves against the enemy. Even in peace, a kingdom should not grow so dull, even if there were no war and no known quarrel. Defenses, musters and preparations should be kept up, assembled and gathered, as if a war were expected. So I say it is right for all of us to go out and inspect the sick and weak parts of France. And let's do it with no show of fear, with no more than if we heard that England was busy with a Whitsun morris-dance. My good lord, England is so idly ruled, and her scepter so carelessly carried by a vain, giddy, shallow, moody youth, that there is nothing to fear from her.

CONSTABLE. Oh, be quiet, Prince Dauphin! You are badly mistaken about this king. Ask Your Grace's recent ambassadors with what great dignity he heard their message, how well supplied he was with noble counselors, how modest in objecting, and yet how terrible in steady resolve. You will find that his past follies were only the outside of the Roman Brutus, covering his good sense with a coat of foolishness. Gardeners do the same when they hide with dung the roots that will sprout first and be the most delicate.

DAUPHIN. Well, it is not so, my Lord High Constable. But even if we think it is, it doesn't matter. When it comes to defense, it's best to judge the enemy to be more powerful than he seems, so that our defenses are fully provided. A weak and stingy plan acts like a miser, who ruins his coat by skimping on a little cloth.

FRENCH KING. Let us think King Harry strong. And, Princes, make sure you arm strongly to meet him. His family has tasted blood against us. He comes from that bloody line that haunted us in our own familiar paths. Remember our shame, which we remember too well, when the battle of Crécy was fought with such fatal result, and all our princes were taken captive by that black name, Edward, the Black Prince of Wales. Meanwhile his mountain of a father stood on a mountain, high up in the air, crowned by the golden sun. He watched his heroic son and smiled to see him mangle the work of nature and deface the patterns that God and French fathers had spent twenty years making. This king is a branch of that victorious stock. Let us fear his natural might and his destiny.
Enter a Messenger.
MESSENGER. Ambassadors from Harry, King of England, ask to be admitted to Your Majesty.
FRENCH KING. We'll give them an audience at once. Go and bring them.
[_Exeunt Messenger and certain Lords._]
You see, friends, this chase is hotly pursued.

DAUPHIN. Turn and stop the pursuit. Cowardly dogs bark most when what they seem to threaten runs far ahead of them. My good sovereign, cut the English short, and let them know what a monarchy you are the head of. Self-love, my lord, is not so vile a sin as self-neglect.
Enter Exeter.
FRENCH KING. From our brother of England?

EXETER. From him. And this is how he greets Your Majesty. In the name of God Almighty, he wills that you give up and set aside the borrowed glories that belong to him and his heirs by gift of heaven, by the law of nature and of nations. Namely, the crown and all the wide-stretching honors that belong by custom and the decree of the ages to the crown of France. So that you may know his is no crooked or clumsy claim, picked from the worm-holes of long-vanished days or raked from the dust of old oblivion, he sends you this memorable family line, truly proven in every branch. He wants you to look over this pedigree. When you find that he is rightly descended from his famous ancestor Edward the Third, he then orders you to give up your crown and kingdom, which you hold only indirectly from him, the natural and true claimant.
FRENCH KING. Or else what follows?

EXETER. Bloody force. Even if you hide the crown in your hearts, he will dig for it there. So he is coming in a fierce tempest, in thunder and earthquake, like a Jove, so that if asking fails, he will compel you. He bids you, in the name of the Lord's mercy, hand over the crown, and take pity on the poor souls for whom this hungry war opens its vast jaws. If you don't, he turns on your head the widows' tears, the orphans' cries, the dead men's blood, and the groans of pining maidens for the husbands, fathers and betrothed lovers who will be swallowed up in this quarrel. This is his claim, his threat and my message. All this holds unless the Dauphin is present here, to whom I bring a greeting too, and say so expressly.
FRENCH KING. As for us, we will think about this further. Tomorrow you shall carry our full intent back to our brother of England.
DAUPHIN. As for the Dauphin, I stand here for him. What does England have for him?

EXETER. Scorn and defiance. Slight regard, contempt, and anything that does not shame the mighty sender, is what he values you at. This is what my king says. If your father's Highness does not sweeten the bitter mockery you sent His Majesty by granting all his demands in full, he will call you to such a hot answer for it that the caves and womb-like vaults of France will scold your trespass and return your mockery in the second echo of his cannon.

DAUPHIN. Say that if my father gives a fair answer, it is against my will. I want nothing but a quarrel with England. To that end, as suited to his youth and vanity, I presented him with the Paris balls.

EXETER. He'll make your Paris Louvre shake for it, even if it were the mistress-court of mighty Europe. And be assured, you'll find a difference, as we his subjects have found with wonder, between the promise of his greener days and the man he is now. Now he weighs time to the last grain. You will read that in your own losses if he stays in France.
FRENCH KING. Tomorrow you shall know our mind in full.
[_Flourish._]
EXETER. Send us off with all speed, or our king may come here himself to ask about our delay. He has already set foot in this land.
FRENCH KING. You will soon be sent off with fair terms. One night is only a small breath and a little pause in which to answer matters of this importance.
[_Exeunt._]
Flourish. Enter Chorus.

CHORUS. So with imagined wings our swift scene flies, moving as fast as thought. Suppose you have seen the well-equipped king at Hampton pier go aboard with his royal company and his brave fleet, whose silken streamers fan the young sun. Play with your imaginations, and in them watch the ship-boys climbing on the hempen ropes. Hear the shrill whistle that gives orders to the confused sounds. Watch the linen sails, driven by the invisible, creeping wind, draw the huge hulls through the furrowed sea, breasting the lofty swell. Oh, just think you stand on the shore and see a city dancing on the restless waves, for that is how this majestic fleet looks as it holds its course to Harfleur. Follow, follow! Grapple your minds to the sterns of this navy, and leave your England as still as dead midnight, guarded by grandfathers, babies and old women, who are either past or not yet come to strength and power. For who is there, with a chin enriched by just one visible hair, who will not follow these chosen and select cavaliers to France? Work, work your thoughts, and see a siege there. Behold the cannon on their carriages, their deadly mouths gaping at girded Harfleur. Suppose the ambassador from the French comes back and tells Harry that the King offers him Katharine his daughter, and with her, as dowry, some petty and worthless dukedoms. The offer does not please him. And now the nimble gunner touches the devilish cannon with his match,
[_Alarum, and chambers go off._]
And down goes everything before them. Still be kind, and fill out our performance with your imagination.
[_Exit._]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 1 — France. Before Harfleur
paragraphs: Alarum. Enter King Henry, Exeter, Bedford, Gloucester and Soldiers, with scaling-ladders.

KING HENRY. Once more unto the breach, dear friends, once more, or close the wall up with our English dead! In peace there's nothing so becomes a man as quiet stillness and humility. But when the blast of war blows in our ears, then imitate the tiger. Stiffen the sinews, summon up the blood, disguise fair nature with hard-faced rage. Then give your eyes a terrible look. Let them peer out through the opening of your head like brass cannon. Let your brow hang over them as fearfully as a battered rock overhangs and juts above its worn base, swilled by the wild and wasteful ocean. Now clench your teeth and flare your nostrils wide, hold your breath hard, and bend every spirit up to its full height. On, on, you noblest English, whose blood comes from fathers proven in war! Those fathers, like so many Alexanders, fought in these parts from morning to evening, and sheathed their swords only when they ran out of enemies. Do not dishonor your mothers. Now prove that the men you called fathers really did beget you. Be a pattern now to men of coarser blood, and teach them how to fight. And you, good yeomen, whose limbs were made in England, show us here the mettle of your pasture. Let us swear that you are worth your breeding, which I do not doubt. For there is none of you so low and base that he has no noble gleam in his eyes. I see you standing like greyhounds in the leash, straining to start. The game's afoot! Follow your spirit, and on this charge cry, "God for Harry! England and Saint George!"
[_Exeunt. Alarum, and chambers go off._]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 2 — The same
paragraphs: Enter Nym, Bardolph, Pistol and Boy.
BARDOLPH. On, on, on, on, on! To the breach, to the breach!
NYM. Please, Corporal, stay. The knocks are too hot, and for my own part, I don't have a spare set of lives. My mood is too hot for this. That's the plain tune of it.
PISTOL. The plain tune is quite right, for moods abound. Knocks come and go. God's vassals drop and die. And sword and shield, in the bloody field, win immortal fame.
BOY. I wish I were in an alehouse in London! I'd give all my fame for a pot of ale and safety.
PISTOL. And I. If wishes could prevail with me, my purpose would not fail with me, but there I'd hurry.
BOY. As regularly, but not as truly, as a bird sings on a bough.
Enter Fluellen.
FLUELLEN. Up to the breach, you dogs! Get going, you cowards!
[_Driving them forward._]
PISTOL. Be merciful, great Duke, to men of clay. Ease your rage, ease your manly rage, ease your rage, great Duke! Good fine fellow, ease your rage. Use gentleness, sweet chick!
NYM. These are good moods! Your honor wins over bad moods.
[_Exeunt all but Boy._]

BOY. Young as I am, I've watched these three swaggerers. I'm servant to all three, but all three together, even if they would serve me, could not be a man to me, because three such clowns don't add up to one man. Bardolph is white-livered and red-faced. That's how he puts on a bold face but doesn't fight. Pistol has a killing tongue and a quiet sword. That's how he breaks words and keeps his weapons whole. Nym has heard that men of few words are the best men, so he scorns to say his prayers, in case he's thought a coward. But his few bad words are matched by just as few good deeds, for he never broke any man's head but his own, and that was against a post when he was drunk. They'll steal anything and call it a prize. Bardolph stole a lute-case, carried it twelve leagues, and sold it for three halfpence. Nym and Bardolph are sworn brothers in thieving, and in Calais they stole a fire-shovel. From that piece of work I knew these men would carry coals, meaning take insults. They'd have me as familiar with men's pockets as with my gloves or handkerchiefs. That goes against my manhood, if I took from another's pocket to put into mine, for that is plain pocketing of wrongs. I must leave them and look for better service. Their villainy turns my weak stomach, so I must throw it up.
[_Exit._]
Enter Gower and Fluellen.
GOWER. Captain Fluellen, you must come to the mines at once. The Duke of Gloucester wants to speak with you.

FLUELLEN. To the mines! Tell the Duke, look you, it is not so good to come to the mines. For, look you, the mines are not according to the disciplines of war. The hollows of them are not big enough. For, look you, the enemy, you may tell the Duke, look you, has dug himself four yards under the countermines. By Jesus, I think he will blow up everything, if there are not better directions.
GOWER. The Duke of Gloucester, who is in charge of the siege, is entirely guided by an Irishman, a very valiant gentleman, in faith.
FLUELLEN. It is Captain Macmorris, is it not?
GOWER. I think it is.
FLUELLEN. By Jesus, he is an ass, as ever lived. I will prove as much to his face. He has no more direction in the true disciplines of the wars, look you, the Roman disciplines, than a puppy-dog.
Enter Macmorris and Captain Jamy.
GOWER. Here he comes, and the Scots captain, Captain Jamy, with him.

FLUELLEN. Captain Jamy is a marvelously valorous gentleman, that is certain. He has great skill and knowledge in the ancient wars, from my own particular knowledge of his directions. By Jesus, he will argue his case as well as any military man in the world, on the disciplines of the early wars of the Romans.
JAMY. I say good day, Captain Fluellen.
FLUELLEN. Good evening to your worship, good Captain James.
GOWER. How now, Captain Macmorris! Have you left the mines? Have the pioneers given up?

MACMORRIS. By Christ, la! It is badly done! The work is given up. The trumpet sounds the retreat. By my hand I swear, and my father's soul, the work is badly done. It is given up. I would have blown up the town, so Christ save me, la! in an hour. Oh, it is badly done, it is badly done. By my hand, it is badly done!

FLUELLEN. Captain Macmorris, I beg you, will you grant me, look you, a few arguments with you, partly touching or concerning the disciplines of war, the Roman wars, by way of debate, look you, and friendly conversation. Partly to satisfy my opinion, and partly for the satisfaction, look you, of my mind, as touching the direction of military discipline. That is the point.
JAMY. It shall be very good, good faith, good captains both. And I shall repay you with good leave, as I may find occasion. That I shall, by the mass.

MACMORRIS. It is no time to discuss, so Christ save me. The day is hot, and the weather, and the wars, and the King, and the Dukes. It is no time to discuss. The town is besieged, and the trumpet calls us to the breach, and we talk and, by Christ, do nothing. It is a shame for us all. So God save me, it is a shame to stand still. It is a shame, by my hand. And there are throats to be cut and work to be done, and there is nothing done, so Christ save me, la!

JAMY. By the mass, before these eyes of mine take themselves to sleep, I'll do good service, or I'll lie in the ground for it, yes, or go to death. And I'll pay for it as valiantly as I can, that I shall surely do. That is the short and the long of it. By the mass, I would very gladly have heard some argument between you two.
FLUELLEN. Captain Macmorris, I think, look you, under your correction, there are not many of your nation—
MACMORRIS. Of my nation! What is my nation? Is it a villain, and a bastard, and a knave, and a rascal? What is my nation? Who talks of my nation?

FLUELLEN. Look you, if you take the matter differently from how it is meant, Captain Macmorris, perhaps I shall think you do not treat me with the courtesy that, in good sense, you ought to treat me with, look you, since I am as good a man as yourself, both in the disciplines of war, and in the descent of my birth, and in other particulars.
MACMORRIS. I do not know you to be as good a man as myself. So Christ save me, I will cut off your head.
GOWER. Gentlemen both, you are misunderstanding each other.
JAMY. Ah! That's a foul fault.
[_A parley sounded._]
GOWER. The town sounds a parley.
FLUELLEN. Captain Macmorris, when there is a better opportunity to be had, look you, I will be so bold as to tell you I know the disciplines of war. And there's an end of it.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 3 — Before the gates
paragraphs: The Governor and some citizens on the walls; the English forces below. Enter King Henry and his train.

KING HENRY. How does the governor of the town resolve? This is the last parley we will allow. So give yourselves up to our best mercy, or defy us to do our worst, like men proud of their own destruction. For as I am a soldier, which is the name that suits me best in my thoughts, if I begin the bombardment again, I will not leave half-conquered Harfleur until it lies buried in its ashes. The gates of mercy will all be shut. The bloodied soldier, rough and hard of heart, will range free with a bloody hand and a conscience wide as hell, mowing down like grass your fresh young virgins and your blossoming infants. What is that to me, if wicked War, dressed in flames like the prince of fiends, does with his sooty face all the cruel deeds that go with waste and desolation? What is it to me, when you yourselves are the cause, if your pure maidens fall into the hands of hot and forceful rape? What rein can hold licentious wickedness when it runs its fierce course down the hill? We might as uselessly spend our empty commands on enraged soldiers in their plunder as send orders to the leviathan to come ashore. So, you men of Harfleur, take pity on your town and your people, while my soldiers are still under my command, while the cool and gentle wind of grace still blows away the filthy and infectious clouds of reckless murder, plunder and villainy. If not, why, in a moment expect to see the blind and bloody soldier defile with foul hand the hair of your shrill-shrieking daughters. Your fathers will be seized by their silver beards, and their most reverend heads dashed against the walls. Your naked infants will be spitted on pikes, while their mad mothers, with confused howls, split the clouds, as the wives of Jewry did at Herod's bloody-minded slaughtermen. What do you say? Will you yield and avoid this, or be guilty in your defense and be destroyed like this?

GOVERNOR. Our waiting ends today. The Dauphin, whom we begged for help, answers that his forces are not yet ready to lift so great a siege. So, great King, we yield our town and our lives to your gentle mercy. Enter our gates. Dispose of us and ours. We can no longer defend ourselves.

KING HENRY. Open your gates. Come, uncle Exeter, go and enter Harfleur. Stay there and fortify it strongly against the French. Show mercy to them all. As for us, dear uncle, with winter coming on and sickness growing among our soldiers, we will retire to Calais. Tonight we will be your guests in Harfleur. Tomorrow we are ready to march.
Flourish. The King and his train enter the town.

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 4 — The French King’s palace
paragraphs: Enter Katharine and Alice, an old Gentlewoman.
KATHARINE. _Alice, tu as été en Angleterre, et tu parles bien le langage._ — Alice, you have been in England, and you speak the language well. —
ALICE. _Un peu, madame._ — A little, madam. —
KATHARINE. _Je te prie, m'enseignez; il faut que j'apprenne à parler. Comment appelez-vous la main en anglais?_ — Please teach me; I must learn to speak it. What do you call the hand in English? —
ALICE. _La main? Elle est appelée_ — The hand? It is called — de hand.
KATHARINE. De hand. _Et les doigts?_ — And the fingers? —

ALICE. _Les doigts? Ma foi, j'oublie les doigts; mais je me souviendrai. Les doigts? Je pense qu'ils sont appelés_ — The fingers? My faith, I forget the fingers, but I will remember. The fingers? I think they are called — de fingres; _oui_ — yes — de fingres.

KATHARINE. _La main_ — the hand — de hand; _les doigts_ — the fingers — de fingres. _Je pense que je suis le bon écolier; j'ai gagné deux mots d'anglais vitement. Comment appelez-vous les ongles?_ — I think I am a good pupil; I have won two English words quickly. What do you call the nails? —
ALICE. _Les ongles? Nous les appelons_ — The nails? We call them — de nails.
KATHARINE. De nails. _Écoutez; dites-moi, si je parle bien:_ — Listen; tell me if I speak well: — de hand, de fingres, _et_ — and — de nails.
ALICE. _C'est bien dit, madame; il est fort bon anglais._ — That is well said, madam; it is very good English. —
KATHARINE. _Dites-moi l'anglais pour le bras._ — Tell me the English for the arm. —
ALICE. De arm, _madame._ — madam. —
KATHARINE. _Et le coude?_ — And the elbow? —
ALICE. D'elbow.
KATHARINE. D'elbow. _Je m'en fais la répétition de tous les mots que vous m'avez appris dès à présent._ — I will repeat all the words you have taught me so far. —
ALICE. _Il est trop difficile, madame, comme je pense._ — It is too difficult, madam, I think. —
KATHARINE. _Excusez-moi, Alice. Écoutez:_ — Excuse me, Alice. Listen: — d'hand, de fingres, de nails, d'arm, de bilbow.
ALICE. D'elbow, _madame._ — madam. —
KATHARINE. _O Seigneur Dieu, je m'en oublie!_ D'elbow. _Comment appelez-vous le col?_ — Oh Lord God, I forget it! — D'elbow. — What do you call the neck? —
ALICE. De nick, _madame._ — madam. —
KATHARINE. De nick. _Et le menton?_ — And the chin? —
ALICE. De chin.
KATHARINE. De sin. _Le col_ — the neck — de nick; _le menton_ — the chin — de sin.

ALICE. _Oui. Sauf votre honneur, en vérité, vous prononcez les mots aussi droit que les natifs d'Angleterre._ — Yes. With respect, in truth, you pronounce the words as correctly as the natives of England. —
KATHARINE. _Je ne doute point d'apprendre, par la grâce de Dieu, et en peu de temps._ — I do not doubt that I will learn, by the grace of God, and in a short time. —
ALICE. _N'avez-vous pas déjà oublié ce que je vous ai enseigné?_ — Have you not already forgotten what I taught you? —
KATHARINE. _Non, je réciterai à vous promptement:_ — No, I will recite to you promptly: — d'hand, de fingres, de mails,—
ALICE. De nails, _madame._ — madam. —
KATHARINE. De nails, de arm, de ilbow.
ALICE. _Sauf votre honneur_ — With respect — de elbow.
KATHARINE. _Ainsi dis-je_ — So I say — d'elbow, de nick, _et_ — and — de sin. _Comment appelez-vous le pied et la robe?_ — What do you call the foot and the gown? —
ALICE. De foot, _madame; et_ — madam; and — de coun, which to her ear sound like coarse French words.

KATHARINE. De foot _et_ — and — de coun! _O Seigneur Dieu! ils sont les mots de son mauvais, corruptible, gros, et impudique, et non pour les dames d'honneur d'user. Je ne voudrais prononcer ces mots devant les seigneurs de France pour tout le monde. Foh!_ — Oh Lord God! They are words of a bad sound, corrupt, gross and shameless, and not for ladies of honor to use. I would not pronounce those words before the lords of France for anything in the world. Foh! — le foot _et_ le coun! _Néanmoins, je réciterai une autre fois ma leçon ensemble:_ — Nevertheless, I will recite my whole lesson once more together: — d'hand, de fingres, de nails, d'arm, d'elbow, de nick, de sin, de foot, de coun.
ALICE. _Excellent, madame!_ — Excellent, madam! —
KATHARINE. _C'est assez pour une fois. Allons-nous à dîner._ — That is enough for one time. Let us go to dinner. —
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 5 — The same
paragraphs: Enter the King of France, the Dauphin, the Duke of Bourbon, the Constable of France and others.
FRENCH KING. It is certain he has crossed the river Somme.
CONSTABLE. And if he isn't fought, my lord, let us not live in France. Let us give it all up and hand our vineyards to a barbarous people.

DAUPHIN. _O Dieu vivant_! Shall a few sprigs of us, the leftover offspring of our fathers' excess, our cuttings planted in wild and savage stock, shoot up so suddenly into the clouds and look down on the men who grafted them?
BOURBON. Normans, but bastard Normans, Norman bastards! _Mort de ma vie_, if they march on unfought, I will sell my dukedom to buy a slobbery, dirty farm in that corner-thrust island of Albion.

CONSTABLE. _Dieu de batailles_, where do they get this spirit? Isn't their climate foggy, raw and dull? As if in spite, the sun looks pale on them and kills their fruit with frowns. Can soggy water, a drink for over-ridden nags, their barley-broth, boil their cold blood to such valiant heat? And shall our quick blood, fired with wine, seem frosty? Oh, for the honor of our land, let us not hang like drooping icicles on our houses' thatch, while a more frosty people sweat drops of gallant youth in our rich fields! We may call them poor, going by their native lords.
DAUPHIN. By faith and honor, our ladies mock us, and say plainly that our spirit is bred out. They will give their bodies to the lust of English youth, to restock France with bastard warriors.
BOURBON. They send us to the English dancing-schools to learn high lavoltas and swift corantos. They say our grace is only in our heels, and that we are the loftiest runaways.

FRENCH KING. Where is Montjoy the herald? Send him off at once. Let him greet England with our sharp defiance. Up, princes! With a spirit of honor sharper than your swords, hurry to the field! Charles Delabreth, High Constable of France; you Dukes of Orleans, Bourbon and Berry, Alençon, Brabant, Bar and Burgundy; Jacques Chatillon, Rambures, Vaudemont, Beaumont, Grandpré, Roussi and Fauconbridge, Foix, Lestrale, Boucicault and Charolois; high dukes, great princes, barons, lords and knights, for your great seats, now clear yourselves of great shames. Stop Harry of England, who sweeps through our land with banners painted in the blood of Harfleur. Rush on his army as melted snow rushes down on the valleys, whose low, servile position the Alps spit on and pour out their phlegm upon. Go down on him. You have power enough. Bring him to Rouen as our prisoner, in a captive's cart.

CONSTABLE. This is worthy of the great. I am sorry his numbers are so few and his soldiers sick and starving from their march. I am sure that when he sees our army, he will let his heart sink into the sewer of fear and offer us his ransom instead of fighting.
FRENCH KING. So, Lord Constable, hurry Montjoy on his way. Let him tell England that we are sending to learn what ransom he is willing to give. Prince Dauphin, you will stay with us in Rouen.
DAUPHIN. Not so, I beg Your Majesty.
FRENCH KING. Be patient, for you will stay with us. Now go, Lord Constable and all you princes, and quickly bring us word of England's fall.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 6 — The English camp in Picardy
paragraphs: Enter Gower and Fluellen, meeting.
GOWER. How now, Captain Fluellen! Are you coming from the bridge?
FLUELLEN. I assure you, there is very excellent service being done at the bridge.
GOWER. Is the Duke of Exeter safe?

FLUELLEN. The Duke of Exeter is as magnanimous as Agamemnon, and a man whom I love and honor with my soul, and my heart, and my duty, and my life, and my living, and my uttermost power. He is not, God be praised and blessed! hurt in any way, but holds the bridge most valiantly, with excellent discipline. There is an ensign-lieutenant there at the bridge. In my very conscience, I think he is as valiant a man as Mark Antony. And he is a man of no reputation in the world, but I saw him do as gallant service.
GOWER. What do you call him?
FLUELLEN. He is called Ancient Pistol.
GOWER. I don't know him.
Enter Pistol.
FLUELLEN. Here is the man.
PISTOL. Captain, I beg you to do me a favor. The Duke of Exeter loves you well.
FLUELLEN. Yes, I praise God, and I have earned some love from him.

PISTOL. Bardolph, a soldier firm and sound of heart and of lusty valor, has been brought by cruel fate and giddy Fortune's furious, fickle wheel, that blind goddess, who stands upon the rolling, restless stone—

FLUELLEN. By your patience, Ancient Pistol. Fortune is painted blind, with a muffler before her eyes, to show you that Fortune is blind. And she is also painted with a wheel, to show you, which is the moral of it, that she is turning, and inconstant, and changeable, and varying. And her foot, look you, is fixed on a spherical stone, which rolls, and rolls, and rolls. In good truth, the poet gives a most excellent description of it. Fortune is an excellent moral.

PISTOL. Fortune is Bardolph's foe and frowns on him. For he has stolen a pax, and hanged he must be. A damned death! Let the gallows gape for a dog. Let a man go free, and let hemp not choke his windpipe. But Exeter has given the doom of death for a pax of little price. So go and speak. The Duke will hear your voice. Don't let Bardolph's vital thread be cut with the edge of a penny cord and vile reproach. Speak, captain, for his life, and I will repay you.
FLUELLEN. Ancient Pistol, I partly understand your meaning.
PISTOL. Why then, rejoice at it.
FLUELLEN. Certainly, ancient, it is not a thing to rejoice at. For if, look you, he were my brother, I would ask the Duke to do as he pleases and have him executed. For discipline ought to be kept.
PISTOL. Die and be damned! And _fico_ for your friendship!
FLUELLEN. It is well.
PISTOL. The fig of Spain, the insulting gesture.
[_Exit._]
FLUELLEN. Very good.
GOWER. Why, this is an out-and-out counterfeit rascal. I remember him now. A pimp, a cutpurse.
FLUELLEN. I'll assure you, he spoke as brave words at the bridge as you will see on a summer's day. But it is very well. What he has said to me is well, I guarantee you, when the time serves.

GOWER. Why, he is a dupe, a fool, a rogue, who now and then goes to the wars to do himself credit when he returns to London in the guise of a soldier. Such fellows know the great commanders' names perfectly, and they will teach you by heart where actions were fought: at such and such a fort, at such a breach, at such a convoy; who came off bravely, who was shot, who was disgraced, what terms the enemy stood on. They learn all this perfectly in the language of war, and they dress it up with newly minted oaths. What a beard cut like the general's and a horrible camp outfit can do among foaming bottles and ale-soaked wits is wonderful to think about. But you must learn to recognize such slanders on the age, or you may be marvelously mistaken.

FLUELLEN. I tell you what, Captain Gower. I see he is not the man he would like to show the world he is. If I find a hole in his coat, I will tell him my mind. [_Drum heard._] Listen, the King is coming, and I must speak with him about the bridge.
Drum and colours. Enter King Henry, Gloucester and his poor soldiers.
God bless Your Majesty!
KING HENRY. How now, Fluellen! Did you come from the bridge?

FLUELLEN. Yes, if it please Your Majesty. The Duke of Exeter has held the bridge very gallantly. The French have gone off, look you, and there have been gallant and most brave exchanges. Indeed, the enemy had possession of the bridge, but he was forced to retreat, and the Duke of Exeter is master of the bridge. I can tell Your Majesty, the Duke is a brave man.
KING HENRY. What men have you lost, Fluellen?

FLUELLEN. The enemy's losses have been very great, reasonably great. Indeed, for my part, I think the Duke has lost not a single man, except one who is likely to be executed for robbing a church, one Bardolph, if Your Majesty knows the man. His face is all pimples, and welts, and knobs, and flames of fire. His lips blow at his nose, and it is like a coal of fire, sometimes blue and sometimes red. But his nose is executed, and his fire is out.

KING HENRY. We would have all such offenders cut off like that. And we give strict orders that in our marches through the country nothing is to be forced from the villages, nothing taken that is not paid for, and none of the French is to be insulted or abused in scornful language. For when gentleness and cruelty play for a kingdom, the gentler player is the sooner winner.
Tucket. Enter Montjoy.
MONTJOY. You know me by my dress.
KING HENRY. Well then, I know you. What shall I learn from you?
MONTJOY. My master's mind.
KING HENRY. Unfold it.

MONTJOY. This is what my King says. Tell Harry of England: though we seemed dead, we were only sleeping. Waiting for the right moment is a better soldier than rashness. Tell him we could have rebuked him at Harfleur, but we thought it unwise to bruise an injury before it was fully ripe. Now we speak on our cue, and our voice is imperial. England shall repent his folly, see his weakness, and admire our endurance. So let him consider his ransom. It must match the losses we have borne, the subjects we have lost, and the disgrace we have swallowed. His pettiness would bend under the weight of repaying that. For our losses, his treasury is too poor. For the shedding of our blood, the muster of his whole kingdom is too small a number. And for our disgrace, his own person kneeling at our feet would be only a weak and worthless satisfaction. Add defiance to this, and tell him, in conclusion, that he has betrayed his followers, whose condemnation is pronounced. So far my King and master. So much for my office.
KING HENRY. What is your name? I know your rank.
MONTJOY. Montjoy.

KING HENRY. You do your office fairly. Turn back and tell your King I do not seek him now. But I would be willing to march on to Calais without interference. To tell the truth, though it is no wisdom to confess so much to an enemy of craft and advantage, my people are much weakened by sickness, my numbers are reduced, and the few I have are almost no better than that many Frenchmen. Yet when they were healthy, I tell you, herald, I thought one pair of English legs could march three Frenchmen. Still, forgive me, God, that I brag like this! This air of France has blown that vice into me. I must repent. So go and tell your master I am here. My ransom is this frail and worthless body, and my army only a weak and sickly guard. Yet, with God before us, tell him we will come on, though France himself and another neighbor like him stand in our way. Here is something for your trouble, Montjoy. Go and tell your master to think carefully. If we may pass, we will. If we are hindered, we shall discolor your tawny ground with your red blood. And so, Montjoy, farewell. The sum of all our answer is only this. We would not seek a battle as we are. Nor, as we are, will we say we will avoid it. So tell your master.
MONTJOY. I shall deliver it so. Thanks to Your Highness.
[_Exit._]
GLOUCESTER. I hope they will not attack us now.
KING HENRY. We are in God's hands, brother, not in theirs. March to the bridge. It is getting toward night. Beyond the river we'll make camp, and tomorrow tell them to march away.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 7 — The French camp, near Agincourt
paragraphs: Enter the Constable of France, the Lord Rambures, Orleans, Dauphin with others.
CONSTABLE. Bah! I have the best armour in the world. I wish it were day!
ORLEANS. Your armour is excellent, but give my horse his due too.
CONSTABLE. Yours is the best horse in Europe.
ORLEANS. Will morning never come?
DAUPHIN. My Lord of Orleans, and my Lord High Constable, are you talking about horses and armour?
ORLEANS. You are as well supplied with both as any prince in the world.

DAUPHIN. What a long night this is! I would not trade my horse for any other that walks on four pasterns. Hah! He leaps from the ground as if his insides were made of hair. _Le cheval volant_, the Pegasus, _qui a les narines de feu!_ When I get on him, I fly. I am a hawk. He trots on air. The earth sings when he touches it. Even the lowest part of his hoof is more musical than the pipe of Hermes.
ORLEANS. He's the colour of a nutmeg.

DAUPHIN. And as hot as ginger. He is a beast fit for Perseus. He is pure air and fire. The heavy elements of earth and water show up in him only when he stands patiently still while his rider mounts. He is truly a horse, and all other nags you may call beasts.
CONSTABLE. Indeed, my lord, he is a perfect and excellent horse.
DAUPHIN. He is the prince of palfreys. His neigh is like a monarch giving orders, and his look commands homage.
ORLEANS. No more, cousin.

DAUPHIN. No, the man has no wit who cannot find new and well-deserved praise for my palfrey from the lark's rising to the lamb's bedtime. It is a theme as endless as the sea. Turn every grain of sand into an eloquent tongue, and my horse would still give them all something to say. It is a subject for a sovereign to discuss, and for a sovereign's sovereign to ride. The whole world, the familiar part and the unknown part, should put aside its own business and marvel at him. I once wrote a sonnet in his praise and began like this: "Wonder of nature,"—
ORLEANS. I have heard a sonnet begin like that to someone's mistress.
DAUPHIN. Then they copied what I composed for my courser, because my horse is my mistress.
ORLEANS. Your mistress carries you well.
DAUPHIN. Me well, yes, which is the proper praise and perfection of a good and special mistress.
CONSTABLE. No, because I thought yesterday your mistress gave your back a nasty shaking.
DAUPHIN. So perhaps did yours.
CONSTABLE. Mine was not bridled.
DAUPHIN. Oh, then she was probably old and gentle. And you rode her like an Irish foot-soldier, with your French breeches off and in your tight trousers.
CONSTABLE. You have good judgment in horsemanship.
DAUPHIN. Then be warned by me. Men who ride like that, and not carefully, fall into foul bogs. I would rather have my horse for a mistress.
CONSTABLE. I would as soon have my mistress be a nag.
DAUPHIN. I tell you, Constable, my mistress wears her own hair.
CONSTABLE. I could make as true a boast as that, if I had a sow for a mistress.
DAUPHIN. "_Le chien est retourné à son propre vomissement, et la truie lavée au bourbier_." You can make use of anything.
CONSTABLE. Yet I do not use my horse as a mistress, or any such proverb so little to the point.
RAMBURES. My Lord Constable, the armour I saw in your tent tonight: are those stars or suns on it?
CONSTABLE. Stars, my lord.
DAUPHIN. Some of them will fall tomorrow, I hope.
CONSTABLE. And yet my sky will not lack any.
DAUPHIN. That may be, because you wear a great many more than you need, and it would be more honourable if some were gone.
CONSTABLE. Just as your horse carries your praises. He would trot as well if some of your boasts were taken off his back.
DAUPHIN. I wish I could load him with what he deserves! Will day never come? Tomorrow I will trot a mile, and my road will be paved with English faces.
CONSTABLE. I will not say that, for fear I would be faced out of my way. But I wish it were morning, because I am eager to be at the ears of the English.
RAMBURES. Who will bet with me on twenty prisoners?
CONSTABLE. You must first risk yourself before you can have them.
DAUPHIN. It's midnight. I'll go and arm myself.
[_Exit._]
ORLEANS. The Dauphin longs for morning.
RAMBURES. He longs to eat the English.
CONSTABLE. I think he will eat everything he kills.
ORLEANS. By the white hand of my lady, he's a gallant prince.
CONSTABLE. Swear by her foot, so that she can tread the oath out.
ORLEANS. He is simply the most active gentleman in France.
CONSTABLE. Doing is activity, and he is always doing.
ORLEANS. He never did any harm, as far as I have heard.
CONSTABLE. And he won't do any tomorrow. He will keep that good name.
ORLEANS. I know he is valiant.
CONSTABLE. I was told that by someone who knows him better than you do.
ORLEANS. Who is that?
CONSTABLE. Why, he told me himself. And he said he did not care who knew it.
ORLEANS. He doesn't need to. It is no hidden virtue in him.
CONSTABLE. By my faith, sir, it is. Nobody ever saw it but his servant. It is a hooded valour, like a hawk with its hood on, and when it is uncovered it will flap and flinch.
ORLEANS. "Ill will never said well."
CONSTABLE. I will top that proverb with "There is flattery in friendship."
ORLEANS. And I will answer that with "Give the devil his due."
CONSTABLE. Well placed. There stands your friend, the devil. I'll aim at the very eye of that proverb with "A pox on the devil."
ORLEANS. You are better at proverbs by exactly as much as "A fool's arrow is soon shot."
CONSTABLE. You have shot over the mark.
ORLEANS. It's not the first time you were overshot.
Enter a Messenger.
MESSENGER. My Lord High Constable, the English are camped within fifteen hundred paces of your tents.
CONSTABLE. Who measured the ground?
MESSENGER. The Lord Grandpré.
CONSTABLE. A valiant and very expert gentleman. I wish it were day! Alas, poor Harry of England, he does not long for the dawn as we do.
ORLEANS. What a wretched and silly fellow this King of England is, to mope so far from home with his fat-brained followers!
CONSTABLE. If the English had any sense, they would run away.
ORLEANS. They lack that. If their heads had any intellectual armour, they could never wear such heavy helmets.
RAMBURES. That island of England breeds very valiant creatures. Their mastiffs have unmatched courage.

ORLEANS. Foolish dogs, that run blinking into the mouth of a Russian bear and have their heads crushed like rotten apples! You might as well call a flea valiant for daring to eat its breakfast on the lip of a lion.

CONSTABLE. Exactly, exactly. And the men are like the mastiffs in their fierce and rough attack, leaving their wits at home with their wives. Then give them big meals of beef and iron and steel, and they will eat like wolves and fight like devils.
ORLEANS. Yes, but these English are badly short of beef.
CONSTABLE. Then tomorrow we will find they have stomachs only to eat and none to fight. Now it is time to arm. Come, shall we get to it?
ORLEANS. It is two o'clock now. But, let me see, by ten we shall each have a hundred Englishmen.
[_Exeunt._]
Enter Chorus.

CHORUS. Now imagine a time when creeping whispers and the staring dark fill the wide vessel of the universe. From camp to camp, through the foul womb of night, the hum of both armies sounds softly.
