The sentries standing guard can almost hear the secret whispers of the other side's watch. Fire answers fire, and through their pale flames each army sees the other's shadowed face. Horse threatens horse, with high and boastful neighs piercing the dull ear of night. From the tents, the armourers, fitting out the knights, close up rivets with busy hammers and give a dreadful sign of preparation. The country cocks crow, the clocks toll, and they name the third hour of drowsy morning. Proud of their numbers and carefree at heart, the confident and over-eager French play dice for the poorly valued English. They scold lame, slow-footed Night, who limps so tediously away like a foul and ugly witch. The poor condemned English sit patiently by their watchful fires, like sacrifices, and brood inwardly on the morning's danger. Their sad bearing, wrapped around gaunt, lean cheeks and war-worn coats, shows them to the gazing moon as so many horrid ghosts. Now, whoever wants to see the royal captain of this ruined band walking from watch to watch, from tent to tent, let him cry, "Praise and glory on his head!" For the King goes out and visits his whole army. He wishes them good morning with a modest smile and calls them brothers, friends and countrymen. On his royal face there is no sign of what a dreadful army has surrounded him. He does not give one bit of his colour to the weary, watchful night. He looks fresh, and he overcomes weariness with a cheerful look and sweet majesty. So every wretch who was pining and pale before takes comfort from his looks as soon as he sees him. Like the sun, his generous eye gives a gift to everyone, thawing cold fear, so that all, humble and noble alike, see, as far as their unworthiness lets them, a little touch of Harry in the night. And so our scene must fly to the battle, where we shall (oh, the pity of it!) greatly disgrace the name of Agincourt with four or five vile and ragged foils, badly suited to a ridiculous brawl. Yet sit and watch, and think of true things through what their mockeries are.
[_Exit._]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 1 — The English camp at Agincourt
paragraphs: Enter King Henry, Bedford and Gloucester.

KING HENRY. Gloucester, it's true that we are in great danger. So our courage should be all the greater. Good morning, brother Bedford. God Almighty! There is some soul of goodness in evil things, if men would watch for it and distil it out. Our bad neighbour makes us early risers, which is both healthy and good management. Besides, our enemies are our outward consciences. They are preachers to us all, warning us to dress ourselves well for our end. So we can gather honey from the weed and draw a moral lesson from the devil himself.
Enter Erpingham.
Good morning, old Sir Thomas Erpingham. A good soft pillow for that good white head would be better than a rough French turf.
ERPINGHAM. Not so, my liege. This bed suits me better, since I can say, "Now I lie like a king."

KING HENRY. It's good for men to learn to love their present pains from example. That eases the spirit. And when the mind is quickened, no doubt, the body's organs, though dead and lifeless before, break out of their drowsy grave and move again, having shed their old skin, with fresh nimbleness. Lend me your cloak, Sir Thomas. Brothers both, give my regards to the princes in our camp. Wish them good morning from me, and then ask them all to come to my pavilion.
GLOUCESTER. We shall, my liege.
ERPINGHAM. Shall I attend your Grace?
KING HENRY. No, my good knight. Go with my brothers to my lords of England. I and my own heart must debate for a while, and then I want no other company.
ERPINGHAM. The Lord in heaven bless you, noble Harry!
[_Exeunt all but King._]
KING HENRY. God reward you, old heart! You speak cheerfully.
Enter Pistol.
PISTOL. _Qui vous là?_
KING HENRY. A friend.
PISTOL. Explain yourself to me. Are you an officer? Or are you base, common and ordinary?
KING HENRY. I am a gentleman serving in a company.
PISTOL. Do you carry the mighty pike?
KING HENRY. Yes, I do. What are you?
PISTOL. As good a gentleman as the Emperor.
KING HENRY. Then you are better than the King.

PISTOL. The King is a fine fellow, and a heart of gold. A lad full of life, a child of fame, of good parents, and most valiant with his fist. I kiss his dirty shoe, and from my heartstrings I love that lovely bully. What is your name?
KING HENRY. Harry le Roy.
PISTOL. Le Roy! A Cornish name. Are you of the Cornish crew?
KING HENRY. No, I am a Welshman.
PISTOL. Do you know Fluellen?
KING HENRY. Yes.
PISTOL. Tell him I'll knock his leek about his head on Saint Davy's day.
KING HENRY. Don't wear your dagger in your cap that day, in case he knocks that about your head instead.
PISTOL. Are you his friend?
KING HENRY. And his kinsman too.
PISTOL. The _fico_ for you, then!
KING HENRY. I thank you. God be with you!
PISTOL. My name is called Pistol.
[_Exit._]
KING HENRY. It suits your fierceness well.
Enter Fluellen and Gower.
GOWER. Captain Fluellen!

FLUELLEN. So! In the name of Jesus Christ, speak lower. It is the greatest wonder in the whole world when the true and ancient privileges and laws of war are not kept. If you would only take the trouble to study the wars of Pompey the Great, you will find, I promise you, that there is no tittle-tattle or prittle-prattle in Pompey's camp. I promise you, you will find the ceremonies of war, and the care of it, and the forms of it, and the sobriety of it, and the modesty of it, were quite different.
GOWER. Why, the enemy is loud. You can hear him all night.
FLUELLEN. If the enemy is an ass and a fool and a prating fop, is it right, do you think, that we should also, look you, be an ass and a fool and a prating fop? In your own conscience, now?
GOWER. I will speak lower.
FLUELLEN. I pray you and beg you that you will.
[_Exeunt Gower and Fluellen._]
KING HENRY. Though it seems a little old-fashioned, there is much care and valour in this Welshman.
Enter three soldiers, John Bates, Alexander Court and Michael Williams.
COURT. Brother John Bates, isn't that the morning breaking over there?
BATES. I think it is. But we have no great reason to want the day to come.
WILLIAMS. We see the beginning of the day over there, but I think we shall never see the end of it. Who goes there?
KING HENRY. A friend.
WILLIAMS. Under what captain do you serve?
KING HENRY. Under Sir Thomas Erpingham.
WILLIAMS. A good old commander and a very kind gentleman. Tell me, what does he think of our situation?
KING HENRY. He thinks we are like men wrecked on a sandbank, who expect to be washed off by the next tide.
BATES. He hasn't told the King what he thinks?

KING HENRY. No, and it isn't right that he should. Though I say it only to you, I think the King is just a man like me. The violet smells to him as it does to me. The sky looks to him as it does to me. All his senses have only human limits. Set aside his ceremonies, and in his nakedness he appears as only a man. His feelings are set higher than ours, but when they stoop, they stoop on the same wing. So when he sees reason for fear as we do, his fears are, without doubt, of the same flavour as ours. Still, it makes sense that no man should let him see any sign of fear, in case showing it discourages his army.

BATES. He may show whatever outward courage he likes. But as cold as the night is, I believe he would wish himself in the Thames up to his neck. And so would I wish him there, and me beside him, whatever the risk, if only we were out of here.
KING HENRY. On my word, I will say what I truly think of the King: I think he would not wish himself anywhere but where he is.
BATES. Then I wish he were here alone. That way he would be sure to be ransomed, and many poor men's lives would be saved.

KING HENRY. I dare say you don't love him so badly as to wish him here alone, however you say it to test other men's minds. For my part, I think I could not die anywhere so contented as in the King's company, as long as his cause is just and his quarrel honourable.
WILLIAMS. That's more than we know.
BATES. Yes, or more than we should try to find out. We know enough if we know we are the King's subjects. If his cause is wrong, our obedience to the King wipes the crime out of us.

WILLIAMS. But if the cause is not good, the King himself has a heavy reckoning to make. All those legs and arms and heads chopped off in a battle will join together on the last day and all cry, "We died in such a place." Some will be swearing, some crying for a surgeon, some calling on the wives they left poor behind them, some on the debts they owe, some on the children they left unprepared. I am afraid few die well who die in a battle. How can they dispose of anything charitably when blood is their business? Now if these men do not die well, it will be a black matter for the King who led them to it. And to disobey him would go against everything a subject owes.

KING HENRY. So, by your rule, if a son is sent by his father on a trading voyage and dies sinfully at sea, the blame for his wickedness should fall on the father who sent him. Or if a servant, carrying a sum of money on his master's orders, is attacked by robbers and dies with many sins unforgiven, you could call the master's business the author of the servant's damnation. But this is not so. The King is not bound to answer for the particular endings of his soldiers, any more than the father for his son or the master for his servant. They do not intend their death when they intend their service. Besides, no king, however spotless his cause, can settle it by the judgment of swords with soldiers who are all spotless. Perhaps some carry the guilt of planned and plotted murder. Some have seduced virgins with the broken seals of perjury. Some are making the wars their shelter after they have wounded the gentle breast of Peace with pillage and robbery. Now if these men have cheated the law and outrun the punishment at home, though they can outstrip men, they have no wings to fly from God. War is his officer, war is his vengeance. So these men are punished, in the King's quarrel now, for breaking the King's laws before. Where they feared death, they escaped with their lives, and where they thought themselves safe, they perish. Then if they die unprepared, the King is no more guilty of their damnation than he was guilty before of the wickedness for which they are now visited. Every subject's duty belongs to the King, but every subject's soul is his own. So every soldier in the wars should do as every sick man in his bed: wash every speck out of his conscience. If he dies that way, death is a gain for him. If he does not die, the time was blessedly lost that bought such preparation. And in the man who escapes, it would be no sin to think that, because he made God so free an offer, God let him outlive that day to see His greatness and to teach others how to prepare.
WILLIAMS. It's certain that every man who dies badly has the evil on his own head. The King is not to answer for it.
BATES. I do not want him to answer for me, and yet I am determined to fight hard for him.
KING HENRY. I myself heard the King say he would not be ransomed.
WILLIAMS. Yes, he said so to make us fight cheerfully. But when our throats are cut, he may be ransomed, and we none the wiser.
KING HENRY. If I live to see it, I will never trust his word again.

WILLIAMS. You'll get even with him then. That's a dangerous shot from a toy elder-wood gun, a poor private man's displeasure against a monarch! You might as well try to turn the sun to ice by fanning his face with a peacock's feather. You'll never trust his word again! Come, that's a foolish thing to say.
KING HENRY. Your rebuke is somewhat too blunt. I would be angry with you if the time were right.
WILLIAMS. Let it be a quarrel between us, if you live.
KING HENRY. I accept it.
WILLIAMS. How shall I know you again?
KING HENRY. Give me some pledge of yours and I will wear it in my cap. Then, if you ever dare to acknowledge it, I will make it my quarrel.
WILLIAMS. Here's my glove. Give me another of yours.
KING HENRY. There.
WILLIAMS. I will wear this in my cap too. If you ever come to me after tomorrow and say, "This is my glove," I swear by this hand I will give you a box on the ear.
KING HENRY. If I ever live to see it, I will challenge it.
WILLIAMS. You dare as well be hanged.
KING HENRY. Well, I will do it, even if I find you in the King's company.
WILLIAMS. Keep your word. Farewell.
BATES. Be friends, you English fools, be friends. We have French quarrels enough, if you could only count them.

KING HENRY. Indeed, the French may bet twenty French crowns to one that they will beat us, because they carry them on their shoulders. But it is no English treason to cut French crowns, and tomorrow the King himself will be a clipper.
[_Exeunt soldiers._]

Upon the King! Let us lay our lives, our souls, our debts, our anxious wives, our children and our sins upon the King! We must bear it all. Oh, hard condition, born twin to greatness, at the mercy of the breath of every fool, whose sense can feel nothing but his own pain! What endless peace of heart kings must give up that private men enjoy! And what do kings have that private men do not have too, except ceremony, mere public ceremony? And what are you, you idol Ceremony? What kind of god are you, that suffer more mortal griefs than your worshippers do? What are your rents? What is your income? Oh, Ceremony, just show me your worth! What is the soul of the worship you get? Are you anything but position, rank and form, creating awe and fear in other men? In that you are less happy being feared than they are in fearing. What do you often drink, instead of sweet homage, but poisoned flattery? Oh, be sick, great greatness, and tell your Ceremony to cure you! Do you think the burning fever will go out with titles blown at it by flattery? Will it give way to bowing and low bending? When you command the beggar's knee, can you command its health? No, you proud dream, that plays so cunningly with a king's rest. I am a king, and I have found you out. I know that it is not the balm, the sceptre and the orb, the sword, the mace, the imperial crown, the robe woven with gold and pearl, the pompous title that runs before the King, the throne he sits on, nor the tide of pomp that beats upon the high shore of this world. No, not all these, thrice-gorgeous Ceremony, not all these, laid in a majestic bed, can sleep as soundly as the wretched slave. He fills his body, empties his mind, and goes to rest, stuffed with bread earned in hardship. He never sees horrid night, the child of hell. Like a servant, from sunrise to sunset he sweats in the eye of Phoebus, and all night he sleeps in Elysium. The next day, after dawn, he rises and helps Hyperion to his horse, and so follows the ever-running year with profitable labour to his grave. And except for ceremony, such a wretch, winding up his days with toil and his nights with sleep, would have the advantage over a king. The slave, a member of the country's peace, enjoys it, but in his thick brain he hardly knows what watch the King keeps to maintain that peace, whose hours the peasant benefits from most.
Enter Erpingham.
ERPINGHAM. My lord, your nobles are worried by your absence and are searching through your camp to find you.
KING HENRY. Good old knight, gather them all together at my tent. I'll be there before you.
ERPINGHAM. I shall do it, my lord.
[_Exit._]

KING HENRY. Oh God of battles! Steel my soldiers' hearts. Do not fill them with fear. Take from them now the sense of counting, if the numbers against them tear their hearts from them. Not today, O Lord, oh, not today, do not think of the fault my father made in getting the crown! I have buried Richard's body again, and I have shed more contrite tears on it than the drops of blood that were forced from it. I have five hundred poor people on yearly pay, who twice a day hold up their withered hands toward heaven to ask pardon for that blood. I have built two chantries, where sad and solemn priests still sing for Richard's soul. I will do more. Though all I can do is worth nothing, since my penitence comes after everything, begging pardon.
Enter Gloucester.
GLOUCESTER. My liege!
KING HENRY. My brother Gloucester's voice? Yes. I know your errand. I will go with you. The day, my friends, and everything else is waiting for me.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 2 — The French camp
paragraphs: Enter the Dauphin, Orleans, Rambures and others.
ORLEANS. The sun is gilding our armour. Up, my lords!
DAUPHIN. _Monte à cheval!_ My horse, _varlet! laquais_, ha!
ORLEANS. Oh, brave spirit!
DAUPHIN. _Via, les eaux et terre!_
ORLEANS. _Rien puis? L'air et feu?_
DAUPHIN. _Cieux_, cousin Orleans.
Enter Constable.
Now, my Lord Constable!
CONSTABLE. Listen to how our horses neigh for service right now!
DAUPHIN. Mount them and cut into their hides, so their hot blood spurts into English eyes and blinds them with more courage than they need, ha!
RAMBURES. What, do you want them to weep our horses' blood? Then how will we see their natural tears?
Enter a Messenger.
MESSENGER. The English are drawn up in battle order, you French peers.

CONSTABLE. To horse, you gallant princes! Straight to horse! Just look at that poor, starved band over there. Your fine show will suck away their souls and leave them only the shells and husks of men. There is not enough work for all our hands. There is scarcely enough blood in all their sickly veins to stain each naked cutlass that our French gallants will draw today and sheathe again for lack of sport. Let us only blow on them, and the vapour of our valour will knock them over. It is certain beyond all exception, lords, that our spare servants and peasants, who swarm uselessly around our battle squares, would be enough to clear this field of such a worthless enemy. We could even stand at the foot of this mountain nearby just to watch, except that our honour will not allow it. What is there to say? Let us do a very, very little, and it is all done. Then let the trumpets sound the tucket call and the signal to mount. Our approach will so challenge the field that England will crouch down in fear and yield.
Enter Grandpré.

GRANDPRÉ. Why do you wait so long, my lords of France? Those island carcasses, desperate for their bones, look ugly on the morning field. Their ragged banners hang loose and sorry, and our air shakes them very scornfully. Great Mars seems bankrupt in their beggared army and peeps feebly through a rusty visor. The horsemen sit like fixed candlesticks with torch-staves in their hands. Their poor nags hang their heads, with drooping hides and hips, the slime hanging in ropes from their pale, dead eyes. In their pale, dull mouths the double-ringed bit lies foul with chewed grass, still and motionless. And their heirs, the thieving crows, fly over them, all impatient for their hour. Description cannot find words to show the life of such a battle, in life so lifeless as it looks.
CONSTABLE. They have said their prayers, and they are waiting for death.
DAUPHIN. Shall we go and send them dinners and fresh clothes, and give their fasting horses some fodder, and fight them after that?
CONSTABLE. I am only waiting for my guard. On to the field! I will take the banner from a trumpet and use it for my haste. Come, come, away! The sun is high, and we are wearing out the day.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 3 — The English camp
paragraphs: Enter Gloucester, Bedford, Exeter, Erpingham, with all his host: Salisbury and Westmorland.
GLOUCESTER. Where is the King?
BEDFORD. The King himself has ridden out to look over their army.
WESTMORLAND. They have a full sixty thousand fighting men.
EXETER. That's five to one. And they are all fresh.

SALISBURY. May God's arm strike with us! It's a fearful disadvantage. God be with you, princes all. I'm off to my command. If we don't meet again until we meet in heaven, then joyfully, my noble Lord of Bedford, my dear Lord Gloucester, my good Lord Exeter, and my kind kinsman, warriors all, farewell!
BEDFORD. Farewell, good Salisbury, and good luck go with you!
EXETER. Farewell, kind lord. Fight valiantly today! And yet I wrong you by reminding you of it, because you are built of the firm truth of valour.
[_Exit Salisbury._]
BEDFORD. He is as full of valour as he is of kindness, princely in both.
Enter the King.
WESTMORLAND. Oh, if only we had here just ten thousand of those men in England who are doing no work today!

KING. Who is it that wishes that? My cousin Westmorland? No, my fair cousin. If we are marked out to die, we are enough to cause our country a loss. And if we are to live, the fewer men there are, the greater share of honour each has. By God's will, I beg you, wish for not one man more. By Jove, I am not greedy for gold, and I don't care who eats at my expense. It doesn't grieve me if men wear my clothes. Such outward things have no place in my desires. But if it is a sin to covet honour, I am the most offending soul alive. No, truly, my cousin, don't wish for a single man from England. By God's peace, I would not lose as much honour as one more man would, I think, take from my share, not for the best hope I have. Oh, don't wish for one more! Rather, Westmorland, proclaim through my army that any man who has no stomach for this fight may leave. His passport will be made out, and money for the journey put into his purse. We would not want to die in the company of a man who is afraid to die with us. This day is called the feast of Crispian. The man who outlives this day and comes safe home will stand on tiptoe when it is named and rouse himself at the name of Crispian. The man who lives through this day and sees old age will feast his neighbours every year on the eve and say, "Tomorrow is Saint Crispian." Then he will roll up his sleeve and show his scars and say, "I got these wounds on Crispian's day." Old men forget. Yet even if all else is forgotten, he will remember, with additions, what feats he did that day. Then our names, as familiar in his mouth as household words, Harry the King, Bedford and Exeter, Warwick and Talbot, Salisbury and Gloucester, will be freshly remembered in their flowing cups. The good man will teach this story to his son. And from this day to the end of the world, Crispin Crispian will never go by without our being remembered in it: we few, we happy few, we band of brothers. For the man who sheds his blood with me today will be my brother. However vile he is, this day will make him a gentleman. And gentlemen in England, now in bed, will think themselves cursed that they were not here, and will hold their manhood cheap whenever anyone speaks who fought with us upon Saint Crispin's day.
Enter Salisbury.
SALISBURY. My sovereign lord, take your place quickly. The French are boldly set in their battle lines and will charge us with all speed.
KING HENRY. Everything is ready, if our minds are too.
WESTMORLAND. Damn the man whose mind holds back now!
KING HENRY. You don't wish for more help from England, cousin?
WESTMORLAND. By God's will, my liege, I wish that you and I alone, without more help, could fight this royal battle!
KING HENRY. Why, now you have unwished five thousand men, which pleases me better than wishing us one more. You know your places. God be with you all!
Tucket. Enter Montjoy.

MONTJOY. Once more I come to learn from you, King Harry, whether you will now agree to a ransom before your certain defeat. You are so near the gulf that you must be swallowed up. Besides, out of mercy, the Constable asks you to remind your followers to repent, so that their souls may make a peaceful and sweet retreat from these fields, where their poor bodies, wretches, must lie and rot.
KING HENRY. Who has sent you now?
MONTJOY. The Constable of France.

KING HENRY. Please carry my former answer back. Tell them to win me first and then sell my bones. Good God! Why should they mock poor fellows like this? The man who once sold the lion's skin while the beast was alive was killed in hunting him. Many of our bodies will no doubt find graves in our homeland, and on those graves, I trust, a record of this day's work will live on in brass. And those who leave their valiant bones in France, dying like men, will be famous, even if they are buried in your dunghills. There the sun will greet them and draw their honours steaming up to heaven, leaving their earthly parts to choke your country, and the smell of them will breed a plague in France. Mark then the overflowing valour of our English, who, even dead, like a bullet that grazes, break out into a second course of mischief, killing as they fall back into death. Let me speak proudly. Tell the Constable we are only warriors for the working day. Our gaiety and our gilt are all smeared with rainy marching in the painful field. There is not a plume of feather in our army (good proof, I hope, that we will not fly), and time has worn us into shabbiness. But by the mass, our hearts are in good trim. And my poor soldiers tell me that before night they will be in fresher robes, or they will pull the gay new coats over the French soldiers' heads and turn them out of service. If they do this, as, if God pleases, they shall, then my ransom will soon be raised. Herald, save your trouble. Come no more for ransom, gentle herald. They shall have none, I swear, but these my joints. If they get those, as I will leave them to them, they will gain little, tell the Constable.
MONTJOY. I shall, King Harry. And so farewell. You will never hear a herald from us again.
[_Exit._]
KING HENRY. I fear you will come again once more for ransom.
Enter York.
YORK. My lord, I beg you most humbly on my knee for the leading of the vanguard.
KING HENRY. Take it, brave York. Now, soldiers, march on. And as it pleases you, God, arrange the day!
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 4 — The field of battle
paragraphs: Alarum. Excursions. Enter Pistol, French Soldier and Boy.
PISTOL. Surrender, you cur!
FRENCH SOLDIER. _Je pense que vous êtes le gentilhomme de bonne qualité._
PISTOL. _Qualité? Caleno custore me!_ Are you a gentleman? What's your name? Speak up.
FRENCH SOLDIER. _O Seigneur Dieu!_
PISTOL. Oh, "Signieur Dew" must be a gentleman. Listen to my words, O Signieur Dew, and mark them. O Signieur Dew, you die on the point of my fox, my sword, unless you give me a huge ransom.
FRENCH SOLDIER. _O, prenez miséricorde! Ayez pitié de moi!_
PISTOL. Moy won't do. I will have forty moys, or I'll drag your belly-lining out through your throat in drops of crimson blood.
FRENCH SOLDIER. _Est-il impossible d’échapper la force de ton bras?_
PISTOL. Brass, you cur! You damned, lecherous mountain goat, you offer me brass?
FRENCH SOLDIER. _O pardonnez-moi!_
PISTOL. Is that what you say? Is that a ton of moys? Come here, boy. Ask this slave in French what his name is.
BOY. _Écoutez. Comment êtes-vous appelé?_
FRENCH SOLDIER. _Monsieur le Fer._
BOY. He says his name is Master Fer.
PISTOL. Master Fer! I'll fer him, and firk him, and ferret him. Tell him that in French.
BOY. I don't know the French for fer, and ferret, and firk.
PISTOL. Tell him to get ready, because I'm going to cut his throat.
FRENCH SOLDIER. _Que dit-il, monsieur?_
BOY. _Il me commande à vous dire que vous faites vous prêt, car ce soldat ici est disposé tout à cette heure de couper votre gorge._
PISTOL. Owy, cuppele gorge, permafoy, peasant! Unless you give me crowns, brave crowns, you'll be mangled by this sword of mine.
FRENCH SOLDIER. _O, je vous supplie, pour l’amour de Dieu, me pardonner! Je suis le gentilhomme de bonne maison; gardez ma vie, et je vous donnerai deux cents écus._
PISTOL. What does he say?
BOY. He begs you to spare his life. He's a gentleman from a good house, and he'll give you two hundred crowns as his ransom.
PISTOL. Tell him my fury will cool down, and I'll take the crowns.
FRENCH SOLDIER. _Petit monsieur, que dit-il?_
BOY. _Encore qu’il est contre son jurement de pardonner aucun prisonnier; néanmoins, pour les écus que vous lui avez promis, il est content à vous donner la liberté, le franchisement._

FRENCH SOLDIER. _Sur mes genoux je vous donne mille remerciements; et je m’estime heureux que je suis tombé entre les mains d’un chevalier, je pense, le plus brave, vaillant, et très distingué seigneur d’Angleterre._
PISTOL. Explain it to me, boy.
BOY. On his knees he gives you a thousand thanks. He counts himself lucky to have fallen into the hands of a man who, he thinks, is the bravest, most valiant and thrice-worthy _seigneur_ in England.
PISTOL. As I suck blood, I will show some mercy. Follow me!
BOY. _Suivez-vous le grand capitaine._
[_Exeunt Pistol and French Soldier._]

I never heard such a full voice come out of such an empty heart. But the saying is true: "The empty vessel makes the greatest sound." Bardolph and Nym had ten times more courage than this roaring devil from the old play, whose nails anyone can pare with a wooden dagger. Both of them are hanged, and so would he be, if he dared to steal anything boldly. I have to stay with the servant boys and the luggage of our camp. The French could take a good prize from us if they knew about it, because there's nobody to guard it but boys.
[_Exit._]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 5 — Another part of the field
paragraphs: Enter Constable, Orleans, Bourbon, Dauphin and Rambures.
CONSTABLE. _O diable!_
ORLEANS. _O Seigneur! le jour est perdu, tout est perdu!_
DAUPHIN. _Mort de ma vie!_ Everything is confounded, everything! Reproach and everlasting shame sit mocking in our plumes.
[_A short alarum._]
_O méchante Fortune!_ Don't run away.
CONSTABLE. Why, all our ranks are broken.
DAUPHIN. Oh, unending shame! Let's stab ourselves. Are these the wretches we played dice for?
ORLEANS. Is this the king we sent word to, demanding his ransom?

BOURBON. Shame and eternal shame, nothing but shame! Let's die with honor! Back in again, once more! And whoever won't follow Bourbon now, let him go off with his cap in his hand, like a low pimp, and hold the bedroom door while a slave no nobler than my dog defiles his fairest daughter.
CONSTABLE. Disorder has ruined us. Let it be our friend now! Let's go in a heap and offer up our lives.
ORLEANS. There are still enough of us alive on the field to smother the English in our crowds, if anyone could think of some order.
BOURBON. The devil take order now! I'm going into the crowd. Let life be short, or else shame will last too long.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 6 — Another part of the field
paragraphs: Alarum. Enter King Henry and his train, with prisoners.
KING HENRY. We have done well, my thrice-valiant countrymen. But we are not finished yet, because the French still hold the field.
EXETER. The Duke of York sends his regards to Your Majesty.
KING HENRY. Is he alive, good uncle? Three times within this hour I saw him go down, and three times get up again and fight. He was covered in blood from helmet to spur.

EXETER. That is how he lies now, brave soldier, fattening the plain with his blood. Beside him, bloody too, lies the noble Earl of Suffolk, his companion in wounds that won them honor. Suffolk died first. Then York, hacked all over, came to him where he lay soaked in gore. He took Suffolk by the beard and kissed the gashes that gaped bloodily on his face. He cried aloud, "Wait, my cousin Suffolk! My soul will keep yours company to heaven. Wait, sweet soul, for mine, and then we'll fly side by side, as we stayed together in our chivalry on this glorious, hard-fought field." At these words I came over and tried to cheer him up. He smiled in my face, reached out his hand, and with a weak grip said, "Dear my lord, give my service to my sovereign." Then he turned, threw his wounded arm over Suffolk's neck, and kissed his lips. So, wedded to death, he sealed with his blood a testament of noble, dying love. The sweet, gentle way of it forced out of me the tears I would have held back. But I did not have enough of the man in me. All my mother came into my eyes and gave me up to weeping.
KING HENRY. I don't blame you. Hearing this, I have to strike a bargain with my misty eyes, or they will spill over too.
[_Alarum._]
But listen! What new alarm is that? The French have regrouped their scattered men. Then let every soldier kill his prisoners. Pass the word along.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 7 — Another part of the field
paragraphs: Enter Fluellen and Gower.
FLUELLEN. Kill the boys and the luggage! It's expressly against the law of arms. It's as arrant a piece of knavery, mark you now, as could be offered. In your conscience, now, isn't it?

GOWER. It's certain there isn't a boy left alive. The cowardly rascals who ran from the battle did this slaughter. On top of that, they have burned and carried off everything that was in the King's tent. So the King, quite rightly, has ordered every soldier to cut his prisoner's throat. Oh, he's a gallant king!
FLUELLEN. Aye, he was born at Monmouth, Captain Gower. What do you call the town where Alexander the Pig was born?
GOWER. Alexander the Great.
FLUELLEN. Why, I ask you, isn't pig great? The pig, or the great, or the mighty, or the huge, or the magnanimous, all come to the same reckoning, except that the phrase is a little different.
GOWER. I think Alexander the Great was born in Macedon. His father was called Philip of Macedon, as I recall.

FLUELLEN. I think it's in Macedon that Alexander was born. I tell you, Captain, if you look in the maps of the world, I warrant you will find, when you compare Macedon and Monmouth, that the situations, look you, are both alike. There is a river in Macedon, and there is also a river at Monmouth. At Monmouth it's called the Wye, but the name of the other river is out of my brains. No matter, it's as alike as my fingers are to my fingers, and there are salmons in both. If you mark Alexander's life well, Harry of Monmouth's life follows it quite closely, for there are figures in all things. Alexander, God knows and you know, in his rages and his furies and his wraths and his cholers and his moods and his displeasures and his indignations, and also being a little intoxicated in his brains, killed his best friend, Cleitus, in his ales and his angers, look you.
GOWER. Our King is not like him in that. He never killed any of his friends.

FLUELLEN. It's not well done, mark you now, to take the tales out of my mouth before they are made and finished. I speak only in the figures and comparisons of it. Alexander killed his friend Cleitus while he was in his ales and his cups. In the same way Harry of Monmouth, being in his right wits and good judgment, turned away the fat knight with the great belly doublet. He was full of jests and gibes and knaveries and mockeries. I have forgotten his name.
GOWER. Sir John Falstaff.
FLUELLEN. That is he. I'll tell you, there are good men born at Monmouth.
GOWER. Here comes his Majesty.
Alarum. Enter King Henry and forces; Warwick, Gloucester, Exeter with prisoners. Flourish.

KING HENRY. I have not been angry once since I came to France until this moment. Take a trumpet, herald, and ride to the horsemen on that hill over there. If they will fight us, tell them to come down, or else leave the field, because they offend our sight. If they will do neither, we will come to them and make them scatter as fast as stones shot from the old Assyrian slings. Besides, we'll cut the throats of the prisoners we hold, and not one of the men we take will taste our mercy. Go and tell them so.
Enter Montjoy.
EXETER. Here comes the French herald, my liege.
GLOUCESTER. His eyes are humbler than they used to be.
KING HENRY. How now! What does this mean, herald? Don't you know I have already put up these bones of mine as my ransom? Do you come again for ransom?

MONTJOY. No, great King. I come to ask your charitable permission to wander over this bloody field, to count our dead and then bury them, and to sort our nobles from our common men. Many of our princes — woe the while! — lie drowned and soaked in common soldiers' blood. And our peasants drench their limbs in the blood of princes. Their wounded horses stand fetlock-deep in gore and, in wild rage, kick their armored hooves at their dead masters, killing them twice. Oh, give us leave, great King, to look over the field in safety and to dispose of their dead bodies!
KING HENRY. I tell you truly, herald, I don't know whether the day is ours or not. Many of your horsemen are still looking on and galloping over the field.
MONTJOY. The day is yours.
KING HENRY. Praised be God, and not our strength, for it! What is that castle called that stands close by?
MONTJOY. They call it Agincourt.
KING HENRY. Then let us call this the field of Agincourt, fought on the day of Crispin Crispianus.

FLUELLEN. Your grandfather of famous memory, if it please your Majesty, and your great-uncle Edward the Black Prince of Wales, as I have read in the chronicles, fought a most brave battle here in France.
KING HENRY. They did, Fluellen.

FLUELLEN. Your Majesty says very true. If your Majesty remembers it, the Welshmen did good service in a garden where leeks grew, wearing leeks in their Monmouth caps. Your Majesty knows that to this hour that is an honorable badge of the service. And I do believe your Majesty takes no scorn in wearing the leek upon Saint Davy's day.
KING HENRY. I wear it as a memorable honor, for I am Welsh, you know, good countryman.
FLUELLEN. All the water in the Wye cannot wash your Majesty's Welsh blood out of your body, I can tell you that. God bless it and preserve it, as long as it pleases His Grace, and His Majesty too!
KING HENRY. Thanks, my good countryman.

FLUELLEN. By Jesus, I am your Majesty's countryman, I care not who knows it. I will confess it to all the world. I need not be ashamed of your Majesty, praised be God, as long as your Majesty is an honest man.
KING HENRY. God keep me so!
Enter Williams.
Our heralds will go with him. Bring me exact word of the numbers dead on both our sides. Call that fellow over there to me.
[_Exeunt Heralds with Montjoy._]
EXETER. Soldier, you must come to the King.
KING HENRY. Soldier, why do you wear that glove in your cap?
WILLIAMS. If it please Your Majesty, it's the pledge of a man I'm supposed to fight, if he's still alive.
KING HENRY. An Englishman?

WILLIAMS. If it please Your Majesty, a rascal who swaggered at me last night. If he's alive and ever dares to challenge this glove, I have sworn to give him a box on the ear. Or if I see my glove in his cap, which he swore as a soldier he would wear if he lived, I will knock it out of there soundly.
KING HENRY. What do you think, Captain Fluellen? Is it right that this soldier keep his oath?
FLUELLEN. He is a coward and a villain otherwise, if it please Your Majesty, in my conscience.
KING HENRY. It may be that his enemy is a gentleman of high rank, well above the soldier's degree, and too high to answer him.

FLUELLEN. Though he be as good a gentleman as the devil is, as Lucifer and Beelzebub himself, it is necessary, look your Grace, that he keep his vow and his oath. If he is perjured, see you now, then his reputation is that of as arrant a villain and a saucy scoundrel as ever set his black shoe on God's ground and His earth, in my conscience, la!
KING HENRY. Then keep your vow, sirrah, when you meet the fellow.
WILLIAMS. So I will, my liege, as I live.
KING HENRY. Whom do you serve under?
WILLIAMS. Under Captain Gower, my liege.
FLUELLEN. Gower is a good captain, and has good knowledge and is well read in the wars.
KING HENRY. Call him here to me, soldier.
WILLIAMS. I will, my liege.
[_Exit._]

KING HENRY. Here, Fluellen, wear this token for me and stick it in your cap. When Alençon and I were down together, I pulled this glove from his helmet. If any man challenges it, he is a friend to Alençon and an enemy to my person. If you meet any such man, arrest him, if you love me.

FLUELLEN. Your Grace does me as great an honor as any subject could wish for in his heart. I would gladly see the man, with only two legs, who will find himself aggrieved at this glove. That is all. But I would gladly see it once, if it please God in His grace that I might.
KING HENRY. Do you know Gower?
FLUELLEN. He is my dear friend, if it please you.
KING HENRY. Please go and look for him, and bring him to my tent.
FLUELLEN. I will fetch him.
[_Exit._]

KING HENRY. My Lord of Warwick, and my brother Gloucester, follow close at Fluellen's heels. The glove I gave him as a token may perhaps earn him a box on the ear. It is the soldier's. By our bargain I should be wearing it myself. Follow, good cousin Warwick. I judge from his blunt bearing that the soldier will keep his word and strike him. Some sudden mischief may come of it, because I know Fluellen is valiant and, once touched by anger, as hot as gunpowder, and he will quickly return an injury. Follow, and see that no harm comes between them. You come with me, uncle of Exeter.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 8 — Before King Henry’s pavilion
paragraphs: Enter Gower and Williams.
WILLIAMS. I'll bet it's to knight you, Captain.
Enter Fluellen.
FLUELLEN. By God's will and pleasure, Captain, I beg you now, come quickly to the King. There is more good coming toward you, perhaps, than you could dream of.
WILLIAMS. Sir, do you know this glove?
FLUELLEN. Know the glove! I know the glove is a glove.
WILLIAMS. I know this, and so I challenge it.
[_Strikes him._]
FLUELLEN. By God's blood! He is as arrant a traitor as any in the whole world, or in France, or in England!
GOWER. How now, sir! You villain!
WILLIAMS. Do you think I'll break my oath?
FLUELLEN. Stand away, Captain Gower. I will pay treason its wages in blows, I warrant you.
WILLIAMS. I am no traitor.
FLUELLEN. That's a lie in your throat. I charge you in his Majesty's name, arrest him. He's a friend of the Duke of Alençon's.
Enter Warwick and Gloucester.
WARWICK. What's this, what's this! What's the matter?
FLUELLEN. My lord of Warwick, here is — praised be God for it! — a most contagious treason brought to light, look you, as you could wish for on a summer's day. Here is his Majesty.
Enter King Henry and Exeter.
KING HENRY. What's this? What's the matter?
FLUELLEN. My liege, here is a villain and a traitor who, look your Grace, has struck the glove that your Majesty took out of the helmet of Alençon.

WILLIAMS. My liege, this was my glove. Here is the other of the pair. The man I gave it to in exchange promised to wear it in his cap. I promised to strike him if he did. I met this man with my glove in his cap, and I have been as good as my word.

FLUELLEN. Hear now, Your Majesty, saving your Majesty's manhood, what an arrant, rascally, beggarly, lousy knave this is. I hope your Majesty will bear me testimony and witness and vouch that this is the glove of Alençon that your Majesty gave me. In your conscience, now?
KING HENRY. Give me your glove, soldier. Look, here is the other of the pair. It was I, indeed, whom you promised to strike, and you have given me the bitterest words.
FLUELLEN. If it please your Majesty, let his neck answer for it, if there is any martial law in the world.
KING HENRY. How can you make me amends?
WILLIAMS. All offenses, my lord, come from the heart. None ever came from mine that could offend your Majesty.
KING HENRY. It was myself you abused.

WILLIAMS. Your Majesty did not come as yourself. You appeared to me as nothing but a common man. Witness the night, your clothes, your humble manner. And whatever Your Highness suffered in that shape, I beg you to take as your own fault and not mine. If you had been what I took you for, I committed no offense. So I beg Your Highness, pardon me.

KING HENRY. Here, uncle Exeter, fill this glove with crowns and give it to this fellow. Keep it, fellow, and wear it as an honor in your cap until I challenge it. Give him his crowns. And, Captain, you must be friends with him.

FLUELLEN. By this day and this light, the fellow has mettle enough in his belly. Here, there are twelve pence for you. And I pray you to serve God and keep yourself out of brawls and brabbles and quarrels and dissensions, and, I warrant you, it will be the better for you.
WILLIAMS. I will have none of your money.

FLUELLEN. It is given with good will. I can tell you, it will serve to mend your shoes. Come, why should you be so bashful? Your shoes are not so good. It's a good shilling, I warrant you, or I will change it.
Enter an English Herald.
KING HENRY. Now, herald, have the dead been counted?
HERALD. Here is the number of the slaughtered French.
KING HENRY. What prisoners of good rank have been taken, uncle?
EXETER. Charles Duke of Orleans, nephew to the King; John Duke of Bourbon, and Lord Boucicault. Of other lords and barons, knights and squires, a full fifteen hundred, besides common men.

KING HENRY. This list tells me that ten thousand French lie slain in the field. Among them, princes and nobles who bear banners lie dead to the number of one hundred twenty-six. Added to these are eight thousand four hundred knights, esquires and gallant gentlemen, of whom five hundred were only made knights yesterday. So among the ten thousand they have lost, there are only sixteen hundred hired common soldiers. The rest are princes, barons, lords, knights, squires and gentlemen of blood and rank. Here are the names of those nobles of theirs who lie dead: Charles Delabreth, High Constable of France; Jacques of Chatillon, Admiral of France; the master of the Crossbows, Lord Rambures; the Great Master of France, the brave Sir Guichard Dauphin; John, Duke of Alençon; Anthony, Duke of Brabant; the brother of the Duke of Burgundy; and Edward, Duke of Bar. Of lusty earls, Grandpré and Roussi, Fauconbridge and Foix, Beaumont and Marle, Vaudemont and Lestrale. Here was a royal fellowship of death! Where is the number of our English dead?
[_Herald gives him another paper._]

Edward the Duke of York, the Earl of Suffolk, Sir Richard Ketly, Davy Gam, esquire. No one else of name, and of all other men only twenty-five. Oh God, your arm was here! Not to us, but to your arm alone, we ascribe it all! When, without stratagem, but in plain shock and fair play of battle, was there ever such a great loss on one side and such a small one on the other? Take it, God, for it is none but yours!
EXETER. It's wonderful!
KING HENRY. Come, let's go in procession to the village. And let it be proclaimed on pain of death throughout our army that no one is to boast of this or take from God the praise that is His alone.
FLUELLEN. Is it not lawful, if it please your Majesty, to tell how many are killed?
KING HENRY. Yes, Captain, but with this acknowledgment: that God fought for us.
FLUELLEN. Yes, in my conscience, He did us great good.

KING HENRY. Let us perform all the holy rites. Let _Non nobis_ and _Te Deum_ be sung, and let the dead be buried in the earth with charity. Then on to Calais, and then to England, where never from France arrived happier men.
[_Exeunt._]
Enter Chorus.

CHORUS. Allow me, for those who have not read the story, to prompt them. And I humbly ask those who have read it to accept the excuse of time, of numbers, and of the proper course of things, which cannot be shown here in their huge and true life. Now we carry the King toward Calais. Grant that he is there. And once he is seen there, lift him away on your winged thoughts across the sea. Look, the English beach is fenced in by a flood of men, with wives and boys, whose shouts and clapping drown out the deep-voiced sea. The sea, like a mighty usher before the King, seems to be clearing his way. So let him land, and solemnly see him set out for London. Thought moves so swiftly that even now you may imagine him on Blackheath. There his lords wish to have his battered helmet and bent sword carried before him through the city. He forbids it, being free of vanity and self-glorifying pride. He gives all the trophy, sign and show entirely away from himself to God. But now look, in the quick forge and workshop of thought, how London pours out her citizens! The mayor and all his brethren in their best order, like the senators of ancient Rome, with the common people swarming at their heels, go out to fetch in their conquering Caesar. By a lesser but loving comparison, suppose the general of our gracious empress were coming now from Ireland, as in good time he may, bringing rebellion spitted on his sword. How many would leave the peaceful city to welcome him! Much more, and with much more cause, did they welcome this Harry. Now place him in London. As yet the lamentation of the French invites the King of England to stay at home, and so does the coming of the Emperor on behalf of France, to arrange peace between them. And leave out all the events, whatever happened, until Harry's return to France. There we must bring him. And I myself have played the interval, by reminding you that it is past. So put up with abridgment, and let your eyes advance after your thoughts, straight back to France.
[_Exit._]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 1 — France. The English camp
paragraphs: Enter Fluellen and Gower.
GOWER. No, that's right. But why are you wearing your leek today? Saint Davy's day is past.

FLUELLEN. There are occasions and causes why and wherefore in all things. I will tell you as my friend, Captain Gower. The rascally, scabby, beggarly, lousy, bragging knave Pistol, whom you and I and all the world know to be no better than a fellow, look you now, of no merits, came to me yesterday and brought me bread and salt, look you, and told me to eat my leek. It was in a place where I could not start a quarrel with him. But I will be so bold as to wear it in my cap until I see him once again, and then I will tell him a little piece of my wishes.
Enter Pistol.
GOWER. Why, here he comes, swelling like a turkey-cock.
FLUELLEN. It's no matter for his swellings or his turkey-cocks. God bless you, Ancient Pistol! You scurvy, lousy knave, God bless you!
PISTOL. Ha! Are you a madman? Do you thirst, base Trojan, to have me fold up Parca's fatal web, the Fate's thread of your life? Away! The smell of leek turns my stomach.

FLUELLEN. I beseech you heartily, scurvy, lousy knave, at my desires and my requests and my petitions, to eat, look you, this leek. Because, look you, you do not love it, and your affections and your appetites and your digestions do not agree with it, I would ask you to eat it.
PISTOL. Not for Cadwallader and all his goats.
FLUELLEN. There is one goat for you. [_Strikes him._] Will you be so good, scabby knave, as to eat it?
PISTOL. Base Trojan, you shall die.

FLUELLEN. You say very true, scabby knave, when God's will is. I will ask you to live in the meantime and eat your food. Come, there is sauce for it. [_Strikes him._] Yesterday you called me mountain-squire, but today I will make you a squire of low degree. I pray you, fall to. If you can mock a leek, you can eat a leek.
GOWER. Enough, Captain. You have astonished him.
FLUELLEN. I say I will make him eat some part of my leek, or I will beat his head for four days. Bite, I pray you. It is good for your green wound and your bloody coxcomb.
PISTOL. Must I bite?
FLUELLEN. Yes, certainly, and out of doubt and out of question too, and ambiguities.
PISTOL. By this leek, I will take most horrible revenge. I eat and eat, I swear—
FLUELLEN. Eat, I pray you. Will you have some more sauce for your leek? There is not enough leek to swear by.
PISTOL. Quiet your cudgel. You see I eat.

FLUELLEN. Much good may it do you, scabby knave, heartily. No, please, throw none away. The skin is good for your broken coxcomb. When you have occasion to see leeks hereafter, I pray you, mock them. That is all.
PISTOL. Good.
FLUELLEN. Aye, leeks are good. Here, there is a groat to heal your head.
PISTOL. Me a groat!
FLUELLEN. Yes, verily and in truth you shall take it, or I have another leek in my pocket, which you shall eat.
PISTOL. I take your groat as a down payment on revenge.
FLUELLEN. If I owe you anything, I will pay you in cudgels. You shall be a woodmonger and buy nothing from me but cudgels. God be with you and keep you and heal your head.
[_Exit._]
PISTOL. All hell shall stir for this.

GOWER. Go, go. You are a counterfeit, cowardly knave. Will you mock an ancient tradition, begun out of honorable respect and worn as a memorial of the valor of the dead, and then not dare to stand behind any of your words with deeds? I have seen you jeering and galling at this gentleman two or three times. You thought that because he could not speak English in the native fashion, he could not handle an English cudgel. You find it otherwise. From now on, let a Welsh correction teach you a good English character. Fare you well.
[_Exit._]

PISTOL. Is Fortune playing the hussy with me now? I have news that my Doll is dead in the hospital of the French disease, and there my meeting place is quite cut off. I am growing old, and from my weary limbs honor is cudgeled out. Well, I'll turn bawd, and lean a little toward cutpurse with a quick hand. To England I will steal, and there I'll steal. I'll get patches for these cudgeled scars, and swear I got them in the Gallic wars.
[_Exit._]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 2 — France. A royal palace
paragraphs: Enter at one door, King Henry, Exeter, Bedford, Warwick, Gloucester, Westmorland, Clarence, Huntingdon and other Lords. At another, Queen Isabel, the French King, the Princess Katharine, Alice, and other Ladies; the Duke of Burgundy and other French.

KING HENRY. Peace to this meeting, the reason we are all here! To our brother of France and our sister, I wish health and a good day. To our most fair and princely cousin Katharine, I wish joy and every good thing. And you, Duke of Burgundy, who are part of this royal family and who arranged this great gathering, I greet you too. And to the French princes and peers, I wish health to you all!
FRENCH KING. We are very glad to see your face, most worthy brother of England. It is good to meet you. And the same to you, English princes, every one.

QUEEN ISABEL. Brother of England, I hope this good day and this gracious meeting turn out as happily as we are glad now to look you in the eye. Until now those eyes have carried the deadly looks of killing basilisks, aimed at any Frenchman who met them. We hope that poison has lost its power. We hope this day turns all grief and quarrels into love.
KING HENRY. We have come here to say amen to that.
QUEEN ISABEL. I greet you all, English princes.

BURGUNDY. My duty to you both, Great Kings of France and England, and my equal love. Your mightinesses can both bear witness how hard I have worked, with all my wits, effort and strength, to bring you to this meeting and royal conference. My efforts have won this much: you have met face to face, royal eye to royal eye. So let it not shame me if I ask you, before this royal company, what obstacle or hindrance keeps Peace from showing her lovely face in this best garden of the world, our fertile France. Peace is naked, poor and mangled. She is the dear nurse of the arts, of plenty and of joyful births. Alas, she has been chased out of France for too long. All her farming lies in heaps and rots in its own richness. Her vine, which cheers the heart, dies unpruned. Her neat hedges, once evenly woven, now sprout wild twigs, like prisoners overgrown with hair. In her fallow fields the darnel, hemlock and rank fumitory take root, while the plowblade that should tear out such wildness rusts. The smooth meadow used to bring forth freckled cowslip, burnet and green clover. Now it lacks the scythe, and it grows rank and untended. In its idleness it breeds nothing but hateful docks, rough thistles, kecksies and burrs, and it loses both beauty and use. Just as our vineyards, fields, meadows and hedges, failing in their nature, grow wild, so our homes, ourselves and our children have lost, or have had no time to learn, the arts that suit our country. We grow like savages, the way soldiers do who think of nothing but blood. We turn to swearing and grim looks, to untidy dress, and to everything that seems unnatural. You are gathered here to bring us back to our former condition. My speech asks only this: let me know what obstacle stops gentle Peace from driving out these evils and blessing us again as she once did.

KING HENRY. Duke of Burgundy, if you want the peace, and its absence is what lets the faults you described grow, then you must buy it. You must agree fully to all our just demands. You have their terms and details, set down briefly, in your hands.
BURGUNDY. The King has heard them. So far he has given no answer.
KING HENRY. Well, then, the peace you urged so strongly depends on his answer.

FRENCH KING. I have only glanced over the articles with a hasty eye. Please appoint some of your council to sit with us again right now. Then we can look them over more carefully, and we will soon give you our final answer.

KING HENRY. We will, brother. Go, uncle Exeter, and brother Clarence, and you, brother Gloucester. Warwick and Huntingdon, go with the King. Take full power with you to confirm, add to or change anything, in or out of our demands, as your wisdom sees best for our dignity. We will sign whatever you agree. Fair sister, will you go with the princes, or stay here with us?
QUEEN ISABEL. Gracious brother, I will go with them. Perhaps a woman's voice may do some good when they insist too narrowly on the articles.
KING HENRY. But leave our cousin Katharine here with us. She is our main demand, and she is listed in the first rank of our articles.
QUEEN ISABEL. She has my leave.
[_Exeunt all except Henry, Katharine and Alice._]
KING HENRY. Fair Katharine, most fair, will you be kind enough to teach a soldier the words that will reach a lady's ear and plead his love to her gentle heart?
KATHARINE. Your Majesty will mock me. I cannot speak your England.
KING HENRY. Oh fair Katharine, if you love me sincerely with your French heart, I will gladly hear you admit it in halting speech with your English tongue. Do you like me, Kate?
KATHARINE. _Pardonnez-moi_ — forgive me — I cannot tell what "like me" is.
KING HENRY. An angel is like you, Kate, and you are like an angel.
KATHARINE. _Que dit-il? Que je suis semblable à les anges?_ — What does he say? That I am like the angels?
ALICE. _Oui, vraiment, sauf votre Grâce, ainsi dit-il._ — Yes, truly, saving your Grace, that is what he says.
KING HENRY. I did say so, dear Katharine, and I am not ashamed to stand by it.
KATHARINE. _O bon Dieu! les langues des hommes sont pleines de tromperies._ — Oh good God! The tongues of men are full of deceits.
KING HENRY. What does she say, fair one? That the tongues of men are full of deceits?
ALICE. _Oui_ — yes — that de tongues of de mans is be full of deceits. Dat is what de Princess says.

KING HENRY. The Princess is the better Englishwoman. In faith, Kate, my wooing suits your understanding. I am glad you can't speak better English. If you could, you would find me such a plain king that you would think I had sold my farm to buy my crown. I don't know how to dress up love. I can only say straight out, "I love you." If you press me further than that, to say "Do you, truly?", my suit is finished. Give me your answer, in faith, do. Then we clap hands and the bargain is struck. What do you say, lady?
KATHARINE. _Sauf votre honneur_ — saving your honor — I understand well.

KING HENRY. Why, Kate, if you made me write verses or dance for your sake, you would ruin me. For the one I have neither words nor meter, and for the other I have no skill in step, though I have a fair amount of strength in step. If I could win a lady at leap-frog, or by vaulting into my saddle with my armor on my back, I would, if boasting may be pardoned, soon leap into a wife. Or if I could fight with fists for my love, or make my horse prance for her favor, I could lay on like a butcher and stick in the saddle like a monkey, never thrown. But before God, Kate, I can't look lovesick, or gasp out fine speeches, and I have no skill at making protestations. I only have plain oaths, which I never use until I'm pushed, and never break however hard I'm pushed. If you can love a fellow of this kind, Kate, whose face is not worth the sunburn, and who never looks in his mirror for love of anything he sees there, then let your eye be your cook. I speak to you as a plain soldier. If you can love me for this, take me. If not, to say I'd die of it would be true, but die for your love? By the Lord, no. Yet I do love you. And as long as you live, dear Kate, take a man of plain, unminted constancy. He must treat you rightly, because he has no gift for wooing elsewhere. These fellows with endless tongues, who can rhyme their way into ladies' favor, always reason their way out again. What! A speaker is only a prater. A rhyme is only a ballad. A good leg will fail. A straight back will stoop. A black beard will turn white. A curly head will go bald. A fair face will wither. A full eye will sink hollow. But a good heart, Kate, is the sun and the moon. Or rather the sun and not the moon, for it shines bright and never changes, but keeps its course faithfully. If you want such a man, take me. Take me, and you take a soldier. Take a soldier, and you take a king. So what do you say to my love? Speak, my fair one, and speak kindly, I beg you.
KATHARINE. Is it possible that I should love the enemy of France?

KING HENRY. No, it is not possible that you should love the enemy of France, Kate. But in loving me you would love the friend of France. I love France so much that I will not give up a single village of it. I will have it all mine. And Kate, when France is mine and I am yours, then France is yours and you are mine.
KATHARINE. I cannot tell what that is.

KING HENRY. No, Kate? I will tell you in French. I am sure it will cling to my tongue like a newly married wife around her husband's neck, hard to shake off. _Je quand sur le possession de France, et quand vous avez le possession de moi_ — when I have France, and when you have me — wait, let me see, what comes next? Saint Denis help me! — _donc votre est France, et vous êtes mienne_ — then France is yours and you are mine. It is as easy for me, Kate, to conquer the kingdom as to speak that much more French. I will never move you in French, unless it is to make you laugh at me.
KATHARINE. _Sauf votre honneur, le français que vous parlez, il est meilleur que l'anglais lequel je parle._ — Saving your honor, the French that you speak is better than the English that I speak.

KING HENRY. No, faith, it is not, Kate. But my speaking your tongue and your speaking mine, both truly false, must be admitted to be much the same. But Kate, do you understand this much English: can you love me?
KATHARINE. I cannot tell.

KING HENRY. Can any of your neighbors tell, Kate? I'll ask them. Come, I know you love me. Tonight, when you go into your private room, you will question this gentlewoman about me. And I know, Kate, that to her you will run down the very qualities in me that you love in your heart. But, good Kate, mock me mercifully, all the more, gentle princess, because I love you cruelly. If you are ever mine, Kate, as a saving faith inside me says you will be, I will have won you in a scramble, so you must prove a good breeder of soldiers. Shall you and I, between Saint Denis and Saint George, not make a boy, half French and half English, who will go to Constantinople and take the Turk by the beard? Shall we not? What do you say, my fair flower-de-luce?
KATHARINE. I do not know that.

KING HENRY. No, that is for later to know, but for now to promise. Just promise now, Kate, that you will do your best, for your French part, toward such a boy. For my English half, take the word of a king and a bachelor. How do you answer, _la plus belle Katherine du monde, mon très cher et divin déesse?_ — the most beautiful Katherine in the world, my most dear and divine goddess?
KATHARINE. Your Majesty has _fausse_ — false — French enough to deceive the most _sage demoiselle_ — wise young lady — that is _en France_ — in France.

KING HENRY. Now, curse my false French! By my honor, in true English, I love you, Kate. By that same honor I dare not swear that you love me. Yet my blood begins to flatter me that you do, in spite of my poor, unsoftening face. Now, curse my father's ambition! He was thinking of civil wars when he fathered me. So I was made with a stubborn outside and an iron look, and when I come to woo ladies I frighten them. But in faith, Kate, the older I get, the better I will look. My comfort is that old age, that bad keeper of beauty, can do no more damage to my face. You have me, if you have me, at my worst. And you will wear me, if you wear me, better and better. So tell me, most fair Katharine, will you have me? Put off your maidenly blushes. Declare the thoughts of your heart with the look of an empress. Take me by the hand and say, "Harry of England, I am yours." The moment you bless my ear with those words, I will tell you aloud: England is yours, Ireland is yours, France is yours, and Henry Plantagenet is yours. He, though I say it to his face, if he is not the equal of the best king, you will find the best king of good fellows. Come, give me your answer in broken music, for your voice is music and your English is broken. So, queen of all, Katharine, break your mind to me in broken English. Will you have me?
KATHARINE. That is as it shall please _le roi mon père_ — the king my father.
KING HENRY. Why, it will please him well, Kate. It shall please him, Kate.
KATHARINE. Then it shall also content me.
KING HENRY. On that I kiss your hand and call you my queen.

KATHARINE. _Laissez, mon seigneur, laissez, laissez!_ — Stop, my lord, stop, stop! — _Ma foi, je ne veux point que vous abaissiez votre grandeur en baisant la main d'une—Notre Seigneur!—indigne serviteur._ — Truly, I do not want you to lower your greatness by kissing the hand of an — Our Lord! — unworthy servant. — _Excusez-moi, je vous supplie, mon très-puissant seigneur._ — Excuse me, I beg you, my most powerful lord.
KING HENRY. Then I will kiss your lips, Kate.

KATHARINE. _Les dames et demoiselles pour être baisées devant leurs noces, il n'est pas la coutume de France._ — For ladies and young ladies to be kissed before their wedding is not the custom of France.
KING HENRY. Madam my interpreter, what does she say?
ALICE. Dat it is not be de fashion _pour les_ — for the — ladies of France — I cannot tell what is _baiser en_ — to kiss in — Anglish.
KING HENRY. To kiss.
ALICE. Your Majesty _entend_ — understands — bettre _que moi_ — than me.
KING HENRY. Is she saying it is not the fashion for maids in France to kiss before they are married?
ALICE. _Oui, vraiment._ — Yes, truly.

KING HENRY. Oh Kate, nice customs bow to great kings. Dear Kate, you and I cannot be confined within the weak fence of one country's fashion. We are the makers of manners, Kate. The freedom that comes with our rank shuts the mouth of every fault-finder, as I will shut yours, for upholding your country's fussy fashion by denying me a kiss. So, patiently and yielding. [_Kissing her._] You have witchcraft in your lips, Kate. There is more eloquence in one sugar touch of them than in the tongues of the whole French council. They would persuade Harry of England sooner than a general petition from monarchs. Here comes your father.
Enter the French Power and the English Lords.
BURGUNDY. God save your Majesty! My royal cousin, are you teaching our princess English?
KING HENRY. I would like her to learn, my fair cousin, how perfectly I love her. And that is good English.
BURGUNDY. Is she not quick to learn?

KING HENRY. Our tongue is rough, cousin, and my nature is not smooth. I have neither the voice nor the heart of flattery in me. So I cannot conjure up the spirit of love in her so that he appears in his true shape.

BURGUNDY. Forgive the frankness of my joke if I answer you on that. If you want to conjure in her, you must draw a circle. And if you want to conjure up Love in her in his true shape, he must appear naked and blind. Can you blame her, then, a maid still rosy with the virgin crimson of modesty, for refusing to let a naked blind boy appear in her own naked, seeing self? It would be, my lord, a hard bargain for a maid to agree to.
KING HENRY. Yet maidens do shut their eyes and yield, since love is blind and forces them.
BURGUNDY. Then they are excused, my lord, when they do not see what they do.
KING HENRY. Then, my good lord, teach your cousin to consent with her eyes shut.

BURGUNDY. I will wink at her to consent, my lord, if you will teach her to know what I mean. For maids that have been well summered and kept warm are like flies at Bartholomew-tide: blind, though they have their eyes. Then they will put up with handling, though before they would not stand being looked at.
KING HENRY. This lesson ties me to waiting for time and a hot summer. So I will catch the fly, your cousin, at the end of the season, and she must be blind too.
BURGUNDY. As love is, my lord, before it loves.
KING HENRY. So it is. And some of you may thank love for my blindness, since I cannot see many a fair French city because of one fair French maid who stands in my way.
FRENCH KING. Yes, my lord, you see them as in a trick of perspective: the cities turned into a maid. For they are all girdled with maiden walls that no war has entered.
KING HENRY. Shall Kate be my wife?
FRENCH KING. If it pleases you.
KING HENRY. I am content, as long as the maiden cities you speak of wait on her. Then the maid who stood in the way of my wish will show me the way to my will.
FRENCH KING. We have consented to all reasonable terms.
KING HENRY. Is that so, my lords of England?
WESTMORLAND. The King has granted every article. First his daughter, and then all the rest in turn, according to their agreed natures.

EXETER. Only this one he has not yet signed. Your Majesty demands that whenever the King of France has occasion to write about a grant, he must name your Highness in this form and with this title. In French: _Notre très-cher fils Henri, Roi d'Angleterre, Héritier de France_ — our most dear son Henry, King of England, Heir of France. And in Latin: _Praeclarissimus filius noster Henricus, rex Angliae et haeres Franciae_ — our most illustrious son Henry, King of England and heir of France.
FRENCH KING. I have not refused this either, brother, so firmly that your request will not make me let it pass.
KING HENRY. Then I ask you, in love and dear alliance, to let that one article rank with the rest. And on that, give me your daughter.

FRENCH KING. Take her, fair son, and from her blood raise up children for me. May the contending kingdoms of France and England, whose very shores look pale with envy of each other's happiness, stop their hatred. May this dear union plant neighborliness and Christian harmony in their sweet hearts, so that war never again raises its bleeding sword between England and fair France.
LORDS. Amen!
KING HENRY. Now, welcome, Kate. And all of you, bear me witness that here I kiss her as my sovereign queen.
[_Flourish._]

QUEEN ISABEL. God, the best maker of all marriages, join your hearts in one and your realms in one! Man and wife, though two, are one in love. May there be such a marriage between your kingdoms that no ill service or cruel jealousy, which so often troubles the bed of blessed marriage, may ever push in between the pact of these kingdoms and divorce their united league. May English and French receive each other as French and English. God say this Amen!
ALL. Amen!

KING HENRY. Let us prepare for our marriage. On that day, my Lord of Burgundy, we will take your oath and the oath of all the peers, as security for our alliances. Then I shall swear to Kate, and you to me. And may our oaths be well kept and prosperous!
[_Sennet. Exeunt._]
EPILOGUE.
Enter Chorus.

CHORUS. So far, with a rough and quite unable pen, our humble author has followed the story. He has confined mighty men in little room and cut short, in fits and starts, the full course of their glory. This star of England lived greatly in a short time, though short it was. Fortune made his sword, and with it he won the world's best garden, France. He left it to his son as emperor-lord. Henry the Sixth, crowned King of France and England while still in baby clothes, succeeded this king. So many people managed his state that they lost France and made England bleed. Our stage has often shown that story. For their sake, let it be accepted kindly in your fair minds.
[_Exit._]
